items.title: How 3 Java Champions are using GitHub Copilot for increased productivity
items.description: AI coding tools can generate code quickly, but speed alone does not solve the hardest software engineering problems. Developers still need to provide context, validate results, protect maintainability, and remain accountable for what ships. To learn how experienced developers strike that balance, we spoke with three Java Champions, all with over a decade of experience in using Java. They shared concrete examples of using GitHub Copilot in production and open source, along with the practices they use to turn AI-generated output into reliable software. Here are the tips they shared with us. Meet the Java Champions Vlad Mihalcea , founder of Hypersistence and author of the book High-Performance Java Persistence Patrick Baumgartner , software crafter at 42talents with 20+ years of Java experience Frank Delporte , senior technical writer at Azul and maintainer of Foojay.io with 15+ years of Java experience Vlad Mihalcea GitHub profile: @vladmihalcea How has GitHub Copilot helped you recently? I’ve been using it to analyze, design, and implement various features in both Hypersistence Utils and Hypersistence Optimizer. For example, I’ve been wanting for a long time to develop a web application that provides Optimizer event history so we can see how performance improvement efforts are materializing in application performance. Before AI, I kept postponing this task because it would have taken me weeks to develop. But using Copilot is like having a new team member, so I used it to create an app that will ship in the next version of Hypersistence Optimizer. Instead of weeks, this task took just two days to implement. What’s your typical usage? Are you using GitHub Copilot as an IDE plugin or the GitHub Copilot app? I use GitHub Copilot in IntelliJ IDEA because it’s convenient to run while reviewing source code or during a debug session. It’s very useful as a code assistant, and it helps me speed up both investigations and building prototypes for features that need validation. I still review the plans and the code that is generated by AI since their goal is to improve my productivity, not replace me entirely. While AI provides the right answer in many situations, there are still times when the response is not satisfactory and requires my intervention. Can you share some tips and best practices? For example, which skills are you using? I created my own skills so that whatever text Copilot generates looks like something I wrote by hand. This skill captures my voice from 65 of my published articles, so a draft comes back sounding like my blog instead of like a language model. This is really useful when generating documentation for this project, since it lets the LLM learn from 12 years of blogging and provide examples that follow the same principles, such as expressiveness, testability, and simplicity. Throughout my career as a software engineer, I’ve learned that we spend far more time on code maintenance than on creating it. Therefore, because maintenance and stability are critical for existing products, I developed skills that help AI mimic existing code practices in accordance with the principle of least astonishment. One tip is to change the model type based on the type of operation. For thorough thinking, I use Opus with the 1 million context window and Extra High or Max reasoning. However, for simpler tasks, such as generating reports, release notes, or verifying documentation, I use lighter models that consume fewer tokens. Patrick Baumgartner GitHub profile: @patbaumgartner Your work involves coaching teams. What is your approach? A lot of my work happens while the normal business still has to keep running. You cannot stop everything for six months to “transform.” We usually start by solving immediate problems together, understand where the team currently stands, define where we want to go and how we will know that we are improving, and then move there step by step. Depending on the situation, that can mean Software Craft practices such as TDD, refactoring, continuous delivery and XP; architecture and modularisation with Spring Boot, Spring Modulith; Spring Security; optimising Java and Spring Boot applications for containers; or increasingly, agentic engineering. The important part for me is that I work with the team. We make decisions together. I don’t want a team to become dependent on me. Ideally, after some time they no longer need me except perhaps as a sparring partner. And maybe that explains why I find this new generation of AI tools so interesting: I like working with people, learning, experimenting, and solving problems. AI gives us another very powerful tool for doing exactly that. Can you share a good story about how GitHub Copilot has helped you recently? There are actually three very different examples that changed how I think about working with GitHub Copilot. Let’s start with the first one. One was a migration of around 900 teaching slides across 15 presentations from Reveal.js to Marp. These were not simple slides. Many contain code, animations, and even interactive examples where I can change JavaScript live while teaching. More importantly, the presentations had already been battle-tested with students. The flow worked. Losing one small piece could break the story I use in the classroom. Doing that migration manually would probably have taken me a week or more—and realistically, I might simply have avoided doing it because it was such tedious work. With Copilot, I approached it differently. We first analysed the existing material, defined the target, created a migration plan, established constraints, provided examples, and defined what had to remain intact. Then we worked from the big structural changes down into the details. The really important part was verification. items.title: Securing AI agent identity with X.509 PKI on AWS
items.description: When AI agents access databases, APIs, and sensitive business operations, establishing cryptographic identity through X.509 public key infrastructure (PKI) becomes a critical requirement. The core challenge is proving which agent made a request, preventing forgery between agents, and confirming that each agent acts only on behalf of an authorized user. Traditional approaches such as sharing API keys between components or passing OAuth tokens through agent chains fall short of the zero-trust requirements that enterprise deployments demand. Multi-agent AI frameworks increasingly use the Model Context Protocol (MCP) to connect agents to external tools and data sources. MCP defines how a large language model (LLM)-powered agent invokes tools such as database queries or email operations. However, MCP has no built-in authentication standard. It is transport-agnostic by design. This creates a critical gap: Without proper identity mechanisms, any component could impersonate an agent, replay intercepted credentials, or invoke tools without authorization. In this post, we show you how to address this gap using Keyfactor EJBCA combined with AWS services. EJBCA is a PKI platform that supports high-availability deployment, REST API automation, and Online Certificate Status Protocol (OCSP) validation. The reference architecture uses four complementary security mechanisms. First, signed request envelopes provide cryptographic proof-of-possession on every agent call. Second, user-signed delegation assertions authorize agents without sharing credentials. Third, RFC 8693 audience-scoped tokens limit the scope of exposure from any single token disclosure. Fourth, real-time OCSP revocation checking propagates credential changes immediately across all agents. The solution uses Amazon Bedrock for LLM inference through the AWS Strands Agents SDK . While this reference architecture uses a database as the protected resource, the same authentication pattern applies to any MCP-compatible tool server. Complete source code for all examples is available in the accompanying GitHub repository. About Keyfactor EJBCA Keyfactor provides a widely adopted machine identity management platform used by more than 1,500 enterprise customers worldwide, according to Keyfactor. These organizations span financial services, healthcare, manufacturing, and government. Keyfactor helps organizations establish and maintain cryptographic trust through certificate lifecycle management, PKI operations, and machine identity governance. EJBCA Enterprise is Keyfactor’s Certificate Authority (CA) and PKI platform, designed for high-availability deployment and REST API automation. Available as an enterprise product, EJBCA provides X.509 certificate issuance, OCSP validation, certificate revocation list (CRL) distribution, and full certificate lifecycle management through both a web console and REST API. EJBCA supports deployment on-premises, in containers, or on Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2). The partnership between AWS and Keyfactor brings together AWS managed services (Amazon Bedrock, AWS Secrets Manager, Amazon Relational Database Service (Amazon RDS)) with PKI infrastructure that supports certificate lifecycle management, automated enrollment, and real-time revocation. This combination addresses a gap in the AI agent ecosystem. While AWS provides the compute, storage, and AI inference layers, Keyfactor provides the cryptographic identity layer that binds agents to verifiable, revocable, short-lived credentials. This joint reference architecture, developed collaboratively by the AWS and Keyfactor engineering teams, demonstrates how to integrate these technologies. You can adapt the patterns shown here to your own multi-agent deployments. Solution overview The architecture implements three authentication layers, each addressing a different trust boundary in the agent communication chain. These three layers use the four security mechanisms introduced earlier: signed envelopes for proof-of-possession, delegation assertions for credential-free authorization, audience-scoped tokens for exposure limitation, and OCSP for real-time revocation. The mechanisms combine across layers as shown in the following table. Layer Trust boundary Mechanism Validates 1. User Auth User to System OAuth + X.509 cert + delegation minting User identity, credential binding 2. Agent-to-Agent Agent to Agent Signed envelopes (PoP + nonce + timestamp) Caller identity, request freshness, no replay 3. MCP Auth Agent to Tool Server Scoped token + envelope + delegation All identities, authorization chain, OCSP Figure 1 shows the three authentication layers and how credentials flow between the user, agents, and the MCP tool server. The diagram illustrates the separation between user credentials (which stay in the login flow), agent credentials (scoped per agent), and the delegation chain that connects them. Figure 1: Three-layer PKI authentication architecture for AI agent systems on AWS Figure 2 illustrates the detailed traffic flow during a typical user session. It shows the sequence of authentication steps from login through certificate issuance, agent delegation, tool invocation, and session cleanup. items.title: How Eon built multi-cloud investigation with an MCP Gateway on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
items.description: This is a guest post co-written with Roei Zavida from Eon. Independent software vendors (ISVs) building AI-powered products need to connect agents and humans to dozens of operational tools across clouds, each with different authentication models, network boundaries, and access policies. When those tools span AWS, GCP, and Azure simultaneously, the integration surface multiplies. This post describes how Eon used Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. Eon used it to replace per-tool credentials and local Model Context Protocol (MCP) processes with a single authenticated gateway. The result gives developers and autonomous agents unified access to investigation tooling across three clouds. New engineers now reach all their investigation tools in about two minutes instead of the two days it previously took to configure credentials and local MCP servers. About Eon Eon provides the Autonomous Data Foundation for the AI era. The platform discovers and classifies cloud resources across AWS, Azure, and GCP. It provides continuous deduplicated backup that reduces storage costs by up to 50 percent in Eon’s internal measurements. It also detects ransomware and rogue-agent damage and delivers live grounded context for AI agents. All of this runs from a single read-only AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) role, storing data in Apache Parquet and Apache Iceberg formats. Founded by former AWS engineers, Eon runs its software as a service (SaaS) infrastructure on AWS. The challenge Eon’s internal engineering team investigates production incidents across multiple clouds and dozens of operational systems. A crashed Kubernetes pod requires checking container logs, Grafana metrics, the deployment’s GitHub pull request (PR), and cloud-provider health status within the same session. Eon needed to address several key requirements: Credential consolidation — Each new tool added another integration to configure, secure, and rotate, which got harder to keep consistent as the toolset grew. Eliminate local MCP processes — Each developer ran several MCP servers locally, which was hard to standardize and keep current. Identity separation — Engineers accessed each system with role-based permissions, but there was no single place to decide which tools each person or agent could call. Cross-account access without networking overhead — Hosting MCP servers across multiple AWS accounts required virtual private cloud (VPC) peering or AWS PrivateLink per account, multiplying operational cost and setup time. Developer onboarding — New engineers spent roughly 2 days configuring credentials and local MCP servers before investigating their first incident. Agent access — Eon’s autonomous site reliability engineering (SRE) agent (running Claude on Amazon Bedrock) needed the same tool access as humans, but with different permissions. Growing engineering headcount combined with a fast-expanding set of AI tools and MCPs made maintaining credentials and local MCP servers increasingly costly. This pushed Eon toward a centralized solution. Approaches considered Before building on AgentCore, Eon evaluated alternatives: Option 1: Centralized proxy with custom auth Every harness had its own proxy configuration with all the targets. A single reverse proxy aggregating all tools, with a custom authentication layer. This handled credential consolidation but only supported remote MCP and required building and maintaining tool protocol translation, session management, and authorization logic from scratch. The implementation and maintenance burden was significant. Option 2: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway , a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, is a managed gateway with built-in identity federation, Cedar-based authorization policies, and Runtime hosting that converts local MCP servers to remote HTTP endpoints. This addressed all requirements without custom infrastructure. Eon chose Option 2 because it provided identity separation, cross-account connectivity, and policy enforcement as managed capabilities rather than code they would need to build and maintain. These were the only two options on the table. Solution overview Eon deployed the full Amazon Bedrock AgentCore stack: AgentCore Gateway, Policy in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, AgentCore Runtime, and AgentCore Identity, all capabilities of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. The following diagram shows how client requests flow through the authentication layer to a single gateway. The gateway routes authorized tool calls to targets hosted on AgentCore Runtimes across multiple AWS accounts. Figure 1: Eon’s centralized gateway architecture on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore The architecture has five layers: Clients Developers using Claude Code, Cursor, or OpenAI Codex connect to a single MCP URL. An autonomous SRE agent running Claude on Amazon Bedrock connects to the same gateway with a different identity. Identity plane Corporate single sign-on (SSO) federates through Amazon Cognito, which mints the JSON Web Token (JWT) and hands it to the gateway. Amazon API Gateway sits in front as the OAuth entry point for humans, proxying the MCP session. Agents authenticate with Cognito client_credentials grants directly against the gateway. One gateway, least-privilege access A single AgentCore MCP Gateway serves as the company-wide front door. Cedar policies in ENFORCE mode control which principals can invoke which tools. Read operations are available to selected groups, not every authenticated user. Write operations are limited to low-impact collaboration actions, such as commenting on a PR or ticket, and production tools are read-only. items.title: Build a semantic layer for agentic AI on AWS with Denodo and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
items.description: Agentic AI applications need governed access to live enterprise data. That data can live in operational systems, analytical warehouses, SaaS applications, other clouds, or on premises. In the previous post in this series , we built a semantic layer on AWS using Stardog’s knowledge graph over Amazon Aurora and Amazon Redshift. A Strands agent on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore queried that layer. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. This post uses the same customer 360 pattern, but swaps in a different semantic layer implementation and extends the source mix. Two things change here. First, the semantic layer is the Denodo Platform: an AI data layer that provides active context and live, zero-copy access to distributed enterprise data. The agent talks to it in VQL , Denodo’s SQL dialect. Second, the source mix includes an on-premises PostgreSQL database alongside Amazon Aurora and Amazon Redshift, so the federation problem is no longer bounded by an Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC). The rest of the pattern carries over. A foundation model on Amazon Bedrock plans and writes queries. The Denodo MCP Server exposes governed views to the agent through the Model Context Protocol (MCP). Amazon Bedrock AgentCore hosts the agent, terminates inbound authentication, and manages the outbound credential the agent presents to Denodo. Everything the model reasons over lives inside the semantic layer rather than the prompt: the joins, the metric definitions, and the row and column filters that apply to the caller. By the end of this post, you will know: How to federate Amazon Aurora, Amazon Redshift, and an on-premises PostgreSQL database in Denodo into a single customer 360 view an agent can query. How to expose that semantic view to an AgentCore-hosted agent through the Denodo MCP Server, and how to register the MCP Server as an AgentCore Gateway target. How the end user’s identity flows from the enterprise identity provider through AgentCore Identity On-Behalf-Of token exchange to Denodo. How Global Security Policies apply row and column filters at query time. The two deployment options for Denodo on AWS: Agora , the fully managed cloud service, and self-managed installation on Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) or Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS). We assume you’re familiar with the semantic-layer architecture from the previous post: what it is, what it’s for, and why the model plans query without owning the joins. If any of that is new, the previous post covers the ground. The example: Customer 360 with a source outside AWS We stay with the same customer 360 pattern from the previous post. The Stardog C360 Knowledge Kit used in the previous article models an ecommerce retailer with two motivating use cases: understanding churn and identifying customers for auto-enrollment in a rewards program. The schema doesn’t change in this post. What changes is where one table lives: rewards_account sits on an on-premises PostgreSQL cluster rather than in Amazon Aurora with the rest of the customer profile data. That placement isn’t a special case. Enterprise data sources might be outside AWS: on premises, in a SaaS tool like a CRM, or in another cloud. The semantic layer must reach whichever applies. We use on-premises PostgreSQL for the walkthrough that represents data from a third-party application. The Extending to other sources section covers what changes when the source is a SaaS tool, a CRM, or a mainframe. It also covers the other hundreds of data sources that Denodo supports by default . Amazon Aurora (PostgreSQL-compatible): Customer profile Table Key columns customer cid (PK), first_name, last_name, email, ssn, phone, location address id (PK), city, state, zip, street_name credit_card id (PK), cid, card_num, card_type Amazon Redshift: Order history Table Key columns order id (PK), cid, pid, order_date, quantity, price, card product id (PK), name, brand, price, dept On-premises PostgreSQL: Rewards program Table Key columns rewards_account id (PK), cid, account_id, create_date The shared identifier is cid , a plain integer that appears as the primary key in the Aurora customer table. It appears as a non-foreign-key column in the Amazon Redshift order table and the on-premises rewards_account . Within Aurora itself, the customer.location column is an integer foreign key to address.id , which is how the profile joins to the address record. There is no foreign key that spans two engines, and no ETL job to build one. Answers that join customers to their purchases and their rewards enrollment must reconcile cid at query time. A representative question this setup answers: “Which of our top 20 customers by lifetime spend haven’t enrolled in the rewards program yet?” This is the auto-enrollment scenario from the Stardog kit, and it needs profile data from Aurora, lifetime spend from Amazon Redshift, and enrollment status from the on-premises cluster to answer. Denodo plans the federated query at execution time, deciding what to push into Aurora, what to push into Amazon Redshift, what to fetch from the on-premises cluster, and how to combine the results. No data moves between sources, and the semantic layer stays declared once for every consumer to reuse. Denodo terms used in this post Denodo implements the semantic layer as a data virtualization platform. Denodo Virtual DataPort (VDP) is the query engine at the core: it’s where the semantic-layer objects live, where VQL executes, and where access policies evaluate. Design Studio is the browser-based authoring surface for VDP. Every object modeled in this post is defined there. Three object types come up repeatedly. A base view is a mapping between a physical table, API, or file in a source system and a logical view in VDP. One Aurora table maps to one base view. items.title: Build a semantic layer for agentic AI on AWS with Strategy Mosaic and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
items.description: This post is co-written with Zhili Cheng, Principal Product Manager, George Earle, Director, AI Engineering, and Kyler K, Sales Engineer of Strategy. In the first post in this series , we built a semantic layer on AWS using Stardog’s knowledge graph over Amazon Aurora and Amazon Redshift and ran a Strands agent on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore against that layer. The second post kept the same customer 360 (C360) pattern and swapped in Denodo’s data virtualization platform, extending the source mix to include an on-premises PostgreSQL cluster. This post uses the same C360 pattern again, with Strategy Mosaic as the semantic layer. Stardog’s semantic layer is ontology-based: concepts and relationships modeled as RDF, with IRIs as the unit of federation and SPARQL as the query language. Denodo’s is data virtualization: base and derived views composed in VQL. Mosaic’s is dimensional: attributes, hierarchies, facts, and metrics composed through Strategy’s metric expression syntax, with linked models as the unit of federation. That model serves four native protocols from one definition: Model Context Protocol (MCP) for AI agents, JDBC/ODBC over Trino for SQL clients, XMLA for Power BI and Excel, and REST for custom applications. Behind those protocols is a long list of certified data sources . Supported systems include cloud warehouses such as Snowflake and Databricks. Operational databases include Amazon Relational Database Service (Amazon RDS) , Oracle, and SQL Server. Analytical engines include Amazon Athena , Trino, and SAP HANA, and software as a service (SaaS) sources include Salesforce. The linked-model pattern extends beyond the Amazon Redshift and Amazon Aurora pair this walkthrough uses. In this walkthrough, a Strands agent hosted on AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, reaches Mosaic through the MCP endpoint. The joins, metric definitions, and per-caller row and column filters live inside Mosaic, not in the agent prompt. We assume you’re familiar with the semantic-layer architecture from the first post in the series. If any of it is new, the Stardog post covers the ground. By the end of this post, you will know: How to model a C360 domain in Strategy Mosaic across Amazon Redshift and Amazon Aurora using two linked models, with no ETL. How Mosaic’s metric syntax (base, advanced with named filter objects, level qualifiers, and compound) captures the business definitions the agent must reason over. How to expose the model to an AgentCore-hosted Strands agent through the Mosaic MCP server, and how user identity propagates so per-user Row-Level Security (RLS) and Object-Level Security (OLS) hold end-to-end. How to choose between live pushdown and in-memory execution for agent traffic. How to publish the same governed definitions to Power BI, Tableau, notebooks, and custom apps, and how to export them in Apache Ossie format for tools outside Mosaic. The source of truth for the walkthrough is Strategy One (March 2026) , the release when Mosaic access through the MCP server became available by default. Strategy Mosaic terms used in this post A short reference before we get to the model. Mosaic Schema and Mosaic Models . Two modeling paths within one universal semantic layer. Mosaic Schema is the centrally governed enterprise model. Mosaic Models is the self-service, AI-assisted modeling path in Mosaic Studio. Models can map to Schema attributes and inherit dimensions, object ACLs, and RLS. This walkthrough uses Mosaic Models. Model . The top-level artifact within either modeling path. Publishes attributes, metrics, hierarchies, and security rules over physical tables. The walkthrough uses two Mosaic Models, one over Amazon Redshift and one over Aurora, linked together. Attribute . A business entity such as Customer. Carries multiple forms: an ID form for joining and a display form for reading. Mosaic uses forms to resolve names like “Carolyn Inworth” to the underlying cid . Hierarchy . A parent-child relationship between attributes. Category rolls up through parent to Department. Address rolls up to City to State. Fact and metric . A fact is a numeric column. A metric aggregates it. Purchase Amount = price * quantity is a base metric. Metrics can also be advanced (an aggregation qualified by a named condition) or compound (a formula over other metrics). Filter object . A named condition referenced from metrics in angle brackets. [Large Orders] is a filter whose qualification is Purchase Amount > 500 . A metric references without inlining the predicate. Level qualifier . Metric expression syntax that pins aggregation grain. {~+, !Customer+} sets the grain to Customer regardless of how the query is sliced. Model linking . Composition across models on shared attributes (Customer, Time). Mosaic pushes aggregates to each source and joins intermediate results on the linking attributes. Certified model . Only certified models are reachable through the MCP server. Live or in-memory . Two per-model execution modes: live pushdown to the source, or answers from a Mosaic-resident cube. Details later in this post. The example: Customer 360 across Amazon Redshift and Amazon Aurora The C360 pattern from the first two posts stays in place. The schema is adapted from Stardog’s C360 Knowledge Kit , so a reader following the series sees the same entities, keys, and anchor question answered by a different semantic layer. A retail organization has customer records, addresses, credit cards, and rewards enrollment sitting on the operational side, and orders, products, and product categories sitting in the warehouse. Business users want answers that span both without knowing which system holds which fact. Where this post differs is how Mosaic reaches the two sources. items.title: Build a semantic layer for agentic AI on AWS with AtScale and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
items.description: In the first post in this series , we built a semantic layer on AWS using Stardog’s knowledge graph over Amazon Aurora and Amazon Redshift . We ran a Strands agent on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore against that layer. The second post kept the same customer 360 (C360) pattern and swapped in Denodo’s data virtualization platform, extending the source mix to include an on-premises PostgreSQL cluster. This post uses the same C360 pattern again, with AtScale as the semantic layer. AtScale takes a different shape from the first two. The semantic model is dimensional (dimensions, hierarchies, and measures) rather than a graph of triples or a set of views. AtScale authors the model in the Semantic Modeling Language , an open, YAML-based specification versioned in Git, and exposes it simultaneously, from a single deployed model, over three protocols: SQL, XML for Analysis (XMLA), and the Model Context Protocol (MCP). The Strands agent and the business intelligence (BI) tools the enterprise already uses get the same computed answer from the same definitions. The rest of the pattern carries over from the earlier posts. A foundation model on Amazon Bedrock (Anthropic Claude Sonnet 4.6 for the walkthrough) plans and writes queries. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore hosts the Strands agent and manages the outbound credential the agent presents to AtScale. The joins, metric definitions, and row and column filters that apply to the caller live inside the semantic layer rather than the prompt. We assume you’re familiar with the semantic-layer architecture from the first post in the series: what a semantic layer is, what it’s for, and why the model plans queries without owning the joins. If any of that is new, the first post covers the ground. By the end of this post, you will know: How to model a C360 domain in the Semantic Modeling Language (SML): datasets, dimensions and hierarchies, facts, measures, calculated measures, and perspectives, versioned in Git. How AtScale plans a dimensional query against Amazon Redshift, and how AtScale’s autonomous aggregate management accelerates the query patterns an agent generates. How to expose the model to an AgentCore-hosted Strands agent through the AtScale MCP server, and how to register that MCP server with AgentCore Gateway , a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. How the human user’s identity propagates from the enterprise identity provider through AgentCore Identity, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, to AtScale, and how AtScale enforces role-based access control (RBAC), row security, and perspectives at query time. How to deploy AtScale on Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) using the AtScale Helm chart and the AtScale K8S Blueprints repository. The source of truth for the walkthrough is the AtScale C2026.7 release . Where a specific tool name or endpoint applies, we cite the AtScale documentation . The example: Customer 360 on Amazon Redshift The customer 360 pattern from the first two posts stays in place. A retail enterprise has customer records, orders, products, and rewards enrollments spread across systems, and business users want to ask cross-cutting questions without knowing which system holds which fact. The Stardog C360 Knowledge Kit we adapted for the first post in the series models this scenario with Customer, Order, Product, and Address entities joined on an integer cid that appears as a primary key in the customer table and as a plain column in the purchase table. Where this post differs from the first two is where the data physically sits. Stardog and Denodo federate at query time across two engines. AtScale plans a dimensional query as native warehouse SQL and pushes it to one engine per query, so cross-engine data is consolidated upstream. For this walkthrough, all analytical C360 data lives in Amazon Redshift Serverless . Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL remains the operational system of record, and a replication path ( AWS Database Migration Service or Amazon Aurora zero-ETL to Amazon Redshift ) keeps the analytical copy current. The agent queries a single AtScale model that maps to the Amazon Redshift tables. The schema in Amazon Redshift: Table Key columns customer cid (PK), first_name, last_name, email, ssn, phone, location address id (PK), city, state, zip, street_name credit_card id (PK), cid, card_num, card_type rewards_account id (PK), cid, account_id, create_date purchase id (PK), pid, purchase_date, quantity, price, cid, card product id (PK), name, brand, price, dept category id (PK), dept_name, parent vendor id (PK), vendor_name, industry Nine columns of interest across eight tables. cid links customer records to purchases. pid links purchases to products. dept links products to categories. Everything analytical is in Amazon Redshift, so joins push down to native SQL rather than being resolved in the semantic layer or in an extract, transform, and load (ETL) pipeline. A representative question that exercises the whole model: Which of our top 20 customers by lifetime spend haven’t enrolled in the rewards program yet? This is the auto-enrollment question from the Denodo post, carried over so a reader following the series can see the same request answered by a different semantic layer. It touches customer profile, address, purchase history, and enrollment status: one row per customer across four logical entities. AtScale terms used in this post AtScale implements the semantic layer as a dimensional model over a warehouse. items.title: The new economics of enterprise AI
items.description: Imagine your company just discovered electricity. At first only a few machines run on it, and nobody worries about efficiency — consumption is low and the value is obvious. But once electricity becomes infrastructure, every process depends on it, and the question changes from “can we use it?” to “how efficiently are we using it?” Enterprise AI is going through the same shift. What began as isolated chatbot and copilot experiments is becoming a foundational layer of the business, with models, agents, and data increasingly interconnected in production workloads. The important question stops being what a token or GPU-hour costs. It becomes how efficiently the AI environment converts paid capacity into useful business outcomes. That’s the metric worth tracking: effective cost per useful outcome — the total platform, model, operations, and capacity cost required to complete work the business can actually use, whether a resolved request or a completed workflow. Three ways to run AI Utilization is central to the economics. Directing more work to paid-for capacity lowers effective unit cost; idle GPUs, fragmented workloads, and oversized models all raise the cost of every useful result. Enterprises generally choose among three models: A bespoke stack — procuring infrastructure and controls in-house. This approach is flexible, but it creates a continuing burden, since teams must revalidate the environment as models and policies change. On-demand consumption — hyperscalers reduce the assembly burden and suit low or uncertain demand, but charges rise with every prompt or agent action. An integrated private AI platform — owned or dedicated capacity paired with a validated stack. The advantage isn’t free inference; it’s control over efficiency levers like scheduling, model selection, GPU partitioning, and cache management. The right model depends on the workload. APIs can be rational for experimentation or variable demand. As workloads become sustained and business-critical, enterprises need to weigh not just what they consume, but how efficiently they operate the system. Ownership is an operating discipline Buying a Formula 1 race car and parking it in your garage means owning one of the most sophisticated vehicles ever built — but ownership alone doesn’t make you competitive; you still need drivers, mechanics, and track time to justify it. AI infrastructure works the same way. One of the biggest misconceptions in enterprise AI is that owning infrastructure automatically improves economics. Owning GPUs creates the opportunity for better economics, but only if the organization has sufficient demand and operational discipline to keep resources productive. The infrastructure that returns the best ROI isn’t a reference architecture or a bespoke build-out — it’s a fully integrated, qualified stack that lets teams route tasks to the least costly model that meets quality requirements and reuse context through techniques such as KV-cache management, reducing wasted capacity while maintaining responsiveness. Without these practices, committed infrastructure can become stranded capital. With them, rising demand improves economics as fixed costs are amortized across more useful work — increasingly important in agentic systems, where economics are shaped less by any single prompt than by the efficiency of the complete environment. From deployment to value HPE Private Cloud AI is a production-ready foundation combining infrastructure, software, models, tools, governance, and services, reducing the integration burden of operating private AI at scale. Its architecture lets teams manage scheduling, model selection, GPU partitioning, and cache management as operational levers, aligning capacity and service levels with each workload’s requirements. It also includes a 90-day engagement with forward-deployed engineers who help customer teams deploy initial use cases and establish repeatable operating practices. In independent testing commissioned by HPE, an integrated platform serving multiple workloads at high utilization delivered a lower effective cost per token than repeatedly renting equivalent capacity. Actual results will vary based on workload mix and utilization. Measure what matters Token consumption remains useful, but it isn’t a complete measure of AI economics. A fuller enterprise view tracks cost per business-relevant outcome, accelerator utilization, and model choice relative to task complexity. Enterprises already operating private AI should ask how mature their utilization is, and how workload volume will change over the next 12 to 18 months. Those earlier in the journey should build these practices in from the first deployment, so strategy anticipates growth before demand becomes a bottleneck. For low-volume, unpredictable demand, an API or hyperscaler may remain sensible. But as AI becomes a continuous production capability, enterprises have a growing incentive to control utilization, amortize fixed costs, and manage the environment as a long-term operating asset. The strategic question isn’t whether enterprises will pay for AI — it’s whether they will understand, and ultimately own, the economics behind it. items.title: Meta Muse exposes users' personal and business secrets when they share conversations
items.description: Muse, the new general-purpose AI agent from Meta, can expose sensitive information when users share conversations through web links, researchers reported Monday. In response to questions from Ars about the behavior, Meta said it's suspending the sharing feature while the company reviews it and considers making changes. Like many online services, Muse has allowed users to share searches, conversations, images, and similar content with other people. Such share features usually involve clicking an option to create a unique URL that anyone can use to load a page hosting the content. To keep potentially sensitive information from being accessible to unintended people, the URLs typically contain a long sequence of text that can’t be easily guessed. A single query is all that's required Muse, which Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg said last month was “built from the ground up for privacy and security,” seems to take the same precautions. But a central design decision for constructing URLs has made the links easy to discover. As a result, researchers from security firm Claroc said they were able to enumerate 6,800 links Muse users created for sharing conversations with others. After opening a few hundred of them, the researchers found information that was clearly not intended to be publicly available, including: Read full article Comments

items.title: AI adoption by industry shows what other sectors can learn
items.description: The current narrative around artificial intelligence in the workplace is largely driven by Silicon Valley. But treating the tech sector as an island misses the actual trends in technology adoption–tech is just the first industry in line. As generative AI and automation tools mature, the shifts currently reshaping software engineering and product management will inevitably filter into healthcare, education, retail, and manufacturing. The variation in adoption rates today isn’t a sign that non-tech industries are falling behind, but rather a reflection of the different speeds at which industries absorb new workflows. For leaders and their teams outside of tech, this differential pace provides a practical blueprint for how AI adoption unfolds, and where the opportunities lie. The AI adoption spectrum by industry Recent survey data from TripleTen highlights just how stark the current adoption curve is across different sectors of the economy (see Figure 1). Figure 1: The AI adoption curve remains steep across industries, but non-tech industry adoption rates are increasing. Source : TripleTen , 2026 While tech leads the way, finance emerges as a clear second: 48% of finance workers have been asked to use AI chatbots, and 32% have been asked to automate parts of their workflow. This demonstrates how rapidly knowledge work integrates AI once clear use cases emerge. By contrast, sectors like healthcare (18% asked to use chatbots) and education (25%) reflect lower initial exposure. Because these broad industry categories encompass a mix of specialized hands-on professionals, clinical or instructional personnel, and back-office administrative staff, universal adoption was never going to happen overnight. Integrating automated tools into compliance-heavy or human-facing operations requires a more deliberate pace, which is reflected by the lower numbers. The AI skills workers are being asked to learn Across all surveyed industries, 79% of workers report being asked to learn at least one skill they didn’t previously have. Looking at the specific competencies demanded in tech today offers a preview of the skill sets likely to shift into other sectors (see Figure 2). Figure 2: Workforces across industries are learning new skills. Source : TripleTen , 2026 Although some of these sound like niche skills confined to tech, many of them will translate to frontline work across sectors—from hospital systems managing patient logistics to school districts processing administrative reporting. One skill gets less attention than it should. Only 30% of managers and owners call judging whether AI output is right or wrong an absolute must, which puts it sixth on a list of seven. As AI tools reach more industries, this is the skill that catches mistakes before they cause problems. It is also where work experience helps most: To spot a wrong answer, you need to know what the right one looks like. How early AI adoption helps your career Early AI adoption offers clear professional leverage: TripleTen’s survey data shows that when managers learned a new skill or automation process from an employee, 88% of those employee-led AI innovations became standard company practice. In early-adopting industries, employees who identify repetitive administrative tasks and use AI tools to streamline them have a voice in shaping organizational policy. As healthcare networks, educational institutions, and retail operations begin broader rollouts of AI-enabled software, workers who understand how to validate outputs, prompt models, and automate routine tasks will hold a strong advantage. Being the person who can streamline administrative overhead promises better chances for retention, promotions, and wage growth. Ana Riabova, the AI strategy and enablement lead at TripleTen, says, “Everyone talks about saving time, but the real win with early adoption is expanding what you can actually do. People who get ahead are using it to handle things they used to have to hand off. It doesn’t matter how senior or junior you are. You keep your core skills, but suddenly you aren’t boxed in by them anymore.” The AI resource gap: Who pays for training and how workers learn If non-tech industries absorb these tools more gradually, the challenge for workers lies in getting access to quality learning resources. Workers’ out-of-pocket investment in training varies significantly by industry: Tech: $1,758 average (13% spent $0) Finance: $1,664 average (24% spent $0) Healthcare: $990 average (45% spent $0) Education: $883 average (42% spent $0) Nearly half of healthcare and education workers spent nothing out of pocket on professional development last year. Furthermore, tech workers actively leverage a larger variety of learning channels (see Figure 3). Figure 3: Professional development efforts mirror the AI adoption curve. Source : TripleTen , 2026 Tech workers are nearly twice as likely as all workers to use AI chatbots as learning tools (48% vs. 27%), and more than twice as likely as workers outside tech (21%), effectively using AI to accelerate their acquisition of other skills. However, ask workers whom they trust most to teach them a new job skill, and they choose someone currently doing that job (31%). Fewer pick an official certification program (19%), an AI tool (16%), or a university professor (6%). Conclusion The difference in AI adoption rates across industries is not a story of who is succeeding and who is failing. Rather, it’s a timeline of how technology diffuses through an economy. Tech and finance are testing the mechanics of AI integration today. For workers in healthcare, education, retail, and manufacturing, the current phase provides a valuable window to observe which skills generate real productivity gains—allowing them to build those competencies before they become standard industry expectations. This content was produced by TripleTen. It was not written by MIT Technology Review’s editorial staff.

items.title: A visit to Samsung’s massive new semiconductor hub
items.description: _____________ THE PLACE Pyeongtaek, South Korea Generative AI models run on powerful chips known as GPUs, which depend on stacks of specialized memory chips packaged with the processor. To meet growing demand for memory, Samsung is building a massive new semiconductor manufacturing complex in Pyeongtaek, South Korea. Three fabs already operate around the clock, and a fourth is coming online. Construction of a fifth was halted during a drop in demand for memory chips in 2024 but restarted when the AI boom sent demand soaring. It’s just before noon on a Monday, and construction workers are pouring out of Samsung’s fabs in Pyeongtaek, a farming city south of Seoul where rice paddies abut a sprawling chipmaking complex. Thousands of workers, dressed head to toe in black with sky-blue vests, take off helmets bearing their names and fab numbers. They walk to lunch, sweaty and flushed, in chunky sneakers capped with yellow rubber toe guards. Some hop on scooters or motorcycles to get around the campus, which covers an area about the size of New York City’s Central Park. They’ll dine at buffets, diners, and beef stew joints, walking past banners advertising short-term leases for studio apartments. Some stop by real estate offices to inquire, stepping up to the same counters where Samsung’s salaried engineers buy new homes . In front of the fourth fab, I meet Choi Hye-rin, a 35-year-old safety officer, as she wipes her forehead with a handkerchief. At dawn, she boarded one of the shuttle buses that ferry workers in from Songtan, an older, scrappier district. She oversees the safety of a crew responsible for building cable ducts. She writes reports, inspects equipment, and checks the chemicals the workers handle. She’s one of hundreds of women working on site, many employed as spotters who walk ahead of heavy equipment. Safety is a big deal here. After lunch, construction picks right back up. Excavators move past rust-red steel structures rising high under tower cranes. Banners that hang from the highest girders read, “Even if the work runs late, don’t rush.” A giant LED scoreboard announces the winners of a contest for writing a poem about safety. Helmets stickered with a pledge, “I will not work if it’s not safe,” perch atop lockers. The finished fabs glisten from across the street. Along with the cautionary messages, there’s a sense of urgency in the air. Samsung predicts that demand for memory chips will continue to surge through 2028. And for years the company watched its domestic rival SK Hynix pull ahead in the global market for the high-bandwidth models that power Nvidia’s AI accelerators. (Meanwhile, the Taiwanese chipmaker TSMC has dominated the foundry business, manufacturing chips that other companies design.) The Pyeongtaek build-out is Samsung’s attempt to reclaim its lead on memory chips. Although the heat can be brutal and the work zones are crowded, Hye-rin has no plans to leave. “The rate here is higher than other construction sites, and the work is relatively easy,” she says. She gets paid 140,000 won ($97) a day and expects the boom to keep her busy for some time: “You just keep coming back.”

items.title: Spain-Based Startups Advance Regional Innovation With Barcelona Supercomputing Center
items.description: The Barcelona Supercomputing Center (BSC) ’s AI Factory Accelerator Programme, now in full operation following a pilot initiative, gives startups access to sovereign compute, technical support and training to support innovation across industries. Many of these companies are also members of the NVIDIA Inception program for cutting-edge startups — and as of today, access to some of the BSC AI Factory services are available through the NVIDIA Inception portal . NVIDIA Inception complements the BSC AI Factory Accelerator Programme by providing members with training through NVIDIA Deep Learning Institute open courses, business mentoring, venture capital connections and other resources. An upcoming extension of MareNostrum 5 — BSC’s public infrastructure serving scientific and technological innovation, powered by NVIDIA accelerated computing — will deliver supercomputing access through the BSC AI Factory and other AI Factories across Europe. BSC AI Factory is among Europe’s first AI factories and the first in Spain, and has delivered more than 800 services to private and public-sector clients since its April 2025 launch. Read All NVIDIA in Europe Announcements Three Inception members were recently named the BSC AI Factory Accelerator Programme’s AI Champions at the pilot initiative’s demo day: Qatium ’s water-network platform — already used by more than 250 utilities in 16 countries — is now in early production with its Neural Water Intelligence technology, powered by proprietary AI models trained on MareNostrum 5. Built on NVIDIA accelerated computing, the NVIDIA cuGraph library, the NVIDIA PhysicsNeMo framework and NVIDIA Nemotron open models, the technology helps water utilities make better operational decisions every day. OneCareAI , a research spin-off from BSC, used NVIDIA NIM microservices to develop technology designed to identify signs of hidden atrial fibrillation — an irregular heart rhythm — in seemingly normal ECGs, helping clinicians identify patients who may be at risk of stroke before one occurs. Avatia built a voice-first, multi-agent system that provides pharmaceutical companies with agentic coworkers that support sales representatives and give doctors transparent, curated information about medicines, ultimately helping the right treatment reach the right patient sooner. The system taps into NVIDIA NIM microservices, the NVIDIA Nemotron 3 open model family and the open source NVIDIA NeMo Curator library. Other BSC AI Factory startups — Agrikola AI , Elna Health , Lokutor , Montevive AI , Oppy , Pack2Earth and Up2Smart — span precision agriculture, medical imaging and knowledge access, speech services, enterprise security, sales intelligence and sustainable packaging. The cohort reflects the breadth of what advanced intelligence can now unlock: preventing strokes, detecting breast cancer subtypes before biopsy, putting medical knowledge at doctors’ fingertips faster, replacing petroleum-based plastic with biobased compostable materials, protecting crops with robots instead of chemicals and more. Learn more about NVIDIA Inception and the BSC AI Factory Accelerator Programme . Read All NVIDIA in Europe Announcements

items.title: My obituary for programming
items.description: My obituary for programming Jeremy Scheff poignantly captures the key loss caused by coding agents for career programmers who enjoyed the puzzle of developing code: Programming turned into one of the greatest jobs you could imagine. You got paid to work on tricky little logic puzzles. The trickier the puzzle, the more you got paid. But even pretty simple puzzles were worth a lot of money because regular people just couldn't do it! No, they needed us. They would give us a problem and we would solve it the way we wanted. We set the strategy, we made the timeline, we defined what was and was not possible. If you're a programmer who thrives on building working systems and doesn't care too deeply about the problems solved along the way, LLMs are the gift that keeps on giving. If directly solving those problems was a big part of your enjoyment, the loss is very real. Via lobste.rs Tags: programming , careers , ai , generative-ai , llms , coding-agents , deep-blue

items.title: Structured outputs for Anthropic Claude models on Amazon Bedrock
items.description: Amazon Bedrock now supports structured outputs for all Anthropic Claude models, on both the bedrock-runtime and bedrock-mantle endpoints, where the model is available. Whether you call Claude through Boto3 and the bedrock-runtime APIs or through the Messages API and the bedrock-mantle endpoint, you can now receive schema-compliant JSON responses that conform to a defined structure. You no longer need custom parsing, retry logic, or post-processing. Practical applications With structured outputs for Claude on Amazon Bedrock, you can automate reliable, schema-compliant tasks across industries. Examples include extracting every required field from financial earnings reports and compliance documents, parsing clinical notes into Electronic Health Records (EHR), and enriching product catalogs with consistent, validated results. You can also analyze contracts for key terms, parties, and obligations, or power intelligent support ticket routing where intents, sentiments, and entities always match your application’s data model. What changes with structured outputs on Amazon Bedrock Structured outputs use constrained decoding to enforce your JSON schema during token generation, not after the fact. The model doesn’t produce tokens that would violate your schema. This changes output formatting from probabilistic to deterministic. Two complementary mechanisms are now available on both Amazon Bedrock endpoints: Feature Purpose Use case JSON Schema output format Control the model’s response structure Data extraction, report generation, API responses Strict tool use Validate tool parameters against schemas Agentic workflows, function calling, multi-step automation What this means for you Each response is a valid JSON, so you no longer encounter JSON.parse() errors or parsing exceptions. Responses are also type safe: field types are enforced, and required fields are always present. Because outputs always conform to your schema, you don’t need retries to handle schema violations, making your integration more reliable. Structured outputs also constrains responses to only the fields your schema defines, which reduces output token count and can lower inference costs for high-volume workloads. These properties make structured outputs production ready, so you can deploy at scale without additional schema-validation code. Supported models and availability Structured outputs works with batch inference , so you can process large volumes of requests asynchronously while still receiving schema-compliant outputs. On the bedrock-runtime endpoint, it also works with cross-Region inference, so you can use it across AWS Regions without additional setup. If you need responses in real time, you can stream structured responses as typed events. How it works When you make a request with a JSON schema, here’s what happens behind the scenes: Schema validation – Amazon Bedrock validates your JSON schema against the supported JSON Schema Draft 2020-12 subset. Grammar compilation – For new schemas, Amazon Bedrock compiles a grammar artifact (the first request might take slightly longer). Caching – Compiled grammars are cached for 24 hours, making subsequent requests faster. Constrained generation – The model generates tokens that produce valid JSON matching your schema. Performance considerations For performance, the first request with a new schema might take longer because Amazon Bedrock compiles a grammar artifact before generation begins. After that initial compilation, subsequent requests using the same schema run with minimal overhead because the compiled grammar is cached. This cache is scoped to your account and lasts for 24 hours from first access. Changing the structure of your JSON schema invalidates the cache and triggers a fresh compilation, while changing only the name or description fields leaves the cached grammar intact. Getting started: Structured outputs with the InvokeModel API (bedrock-runtime) The InvokeModel API takes the Anthropic-native request body, so the schema goes in output_config.format as a JSON object rather than a JSON string. The following example shows how to extract the structured lead data from a customer email using boto3 with an Anthropic Claude model: Python import boto3 import json REGION = "us-east-1" # Choose your preferred region bedrock_runtime = boto3.client(service_name="bedrock-runtime", region_name=REGION) # Define the JSON schema for structured output schema = { "type": "object", "properties": { "name": {"type": "string", "description": "Customer name"}, "email": {"type": "string", "description": "Customer email address"}, "plan_interest": {"type": "string", "description": "Product plan of interest"}, "demo_requested": {"type": "boolean", "description": "Whether a demo was requested"} }, "required": ["name", "email", "plan_interest", "demo_requested"], "additionalProperties": False } # Make a request with structured outputs via the InvokeModel API # (reusing the schema defined for the Converse example) response = bedrock_runtime.invoke_model( modelId="global.anthropic.claude-sonnet-5-5", body=json.dumps({ "anthropic_version": "bedrock-2023-05-31", "max_tokens": 512, "messages": [ {"role": "user", "content": ( "Paulo Santos (paulo@example.com) is interested in our Enterprise plan " "and wants to schedule a demo for next Tuesday at 2pm." )} ], "output_config": {"format": {"type": "json_schema", "schema": schema}} }) ) body = json.loads(response["body"].read()) # Check the stop reason before parsing if body["stop_reason"] == "end_turn": result_text = next(b["text"] for b in body["content"] if b["type"] == "text") print(json.dumps(json.loads(result_text), indent=2)) elif body["stop_reason"] == "max_tokens": print("Response truncated: increase max_tokens and retry.") JSON { "name": "Paulo Santos", "email": "paulo@example.com", "plan_interest": "Enterprise", "demo_requested": true } The response conforms to your schema. No additional validation is required. items.title: Developers can now access SageMaker Studio through the new AWS experience
items.description: Today, we’re excited to announce that new Amazon SageMaker AI customers can now land inside a fully configured Amazon SageMaker Studio environment in only a few steps after signing up for AWS. You can use a sign-in method that you already have, such as Amazon, Apple, GitHub, Google, or an email address. You don’t need to set up an advanced AWS account, enter a credit card (for most customers), or configure an environment manually. New customers also receive $100 in AWS Free Tier credits that work across SageMaker AI, including model customization, training jobs, Studio notebooks, and endpoint deployments. This post follows on from our previous post, From Hugging Face to Amazon SageMaker Studio in One Click , which introduced deep links from Hugging Face model pages directly into SageMaker Studio workflows. Earlier this year, we also sped up Studio environment creation time from 2 minutes to about 20 seconds and pre-configured model customization permissions in every new Studio domain. Together, these changes removed much of the friction after a developer reached Studio. One major hurdle remained before they got there: creating an AWS account. New customers had to verify an email address, enter contact information, verify a phone number, provide payment details, and select a support plan before they could start building. For individual developers and small startup teams used to signing in and building within a few minutes, that was still a significant barrier. What’s new With this launch, SageMaker Studio is now integrated with the updated AWS sign-in and sign-up experience , which introduces new options for creating and managing AWS accounts along with simplified collaboration. New customers can create an account using an identity that they already have and start building in SageMaker Studio right away. New sign-in experience New customers can now sign up using their Google, GitHub, Apple, or Amazon account, or with an email address, in 2–3 steps. You don’t need to complete the advanced AWS account sign-up, verify a phone number, or enter a credit card (for most customers): Figure 1: The Sign up for AWS page with social sign-on options After you sign up, SageMaker AI automatically creates your Studio environment in about 20 seconds. You then land on the page that matches where you started. For example, you might discover and select a model from Hugging Face for deployment through Deploy on SageMaker AI . Studio then opens the Deployment page with the model pre-configured for endpoint creation: Figure 2: Deploying a Hugging Face model on Amazon SageMaker AI Figure 3: Configuring endpoint settings in SageMaker Studio Up to $200 in Free Tier credits, no credit card required for most customers New customers receive $100 in AWS Free Tier credits that work across SageMaker AI, including endpoint deployments, model customization, Studio notebooks, and model training. You also have the chance to earn an additional $100 worth of credits. Credits are applied automatically to your usage, and you receive an email notification as you approach your limit. The Free Tier period ends after 6 months or when you’ve used all your credits, whichever comes first. At that point, resource usage stops automatically, so you won’t be surprised by unexpected charges. You can upgrade to a paid plan at any time by adding payment details. Built on the foundations of previous launches New environments created through the new sign-in experience include the improvements from earlier launches. Permissions for model customization, training, evaluation, and deployment are pre-configured, so you don’t need to create AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) roles. Eligible accounts get default access to G5, G6, and G4dn GPU instances for endpoints, training jobs, and Studio notebooks. Additionally, the instance selection menu in Studio shows quota availability, so you can quickly see which instance types are available for use. Getting started You can try the new sign-in experience today: Browse models on Hugging Face , choose Deploy , select Amazon SageMaker AI and then choose Customize on SageMaker AI or Deploy on SageMaker AI on a supported model. Alternatively, visit the Amazon SageMaker Studio page and choose Get started with Amazon SageMaker AI . On the AWS sign-in page, choose Google , GitHub , Apple , or Amazon , or enter your email address, and follow the prompts to create your account in a few steps. Land in your fully configured SageMaker Studio environment and start building with your Free Tier credits. The new sign-in experience is available for new AWS accounts. If you already have an AWS account, there’s no change to how you sign in. Conclusion The new sign-in experience removes the last major hurdle between discovering and building with Amazon SageMaker AI. Combined with faster environment creation, pre-configured permissions, deep links from Hugging Face, and default GPU access, individual developers can get started quickly. Startup teams can now go from finding a model to customizing or deploying it in minutes, using an identity they already have. To get started, visit aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/studio or explore models on Hugging Face . About the authors Hazim Qudah Hazim is a Specialist Solutions Architect at AWS based in Dallas, TX. He enjoys helping customers build and adopt AI/ML solutions using AWS technologies and best practices. Prior to his role at AWS, he spent many years in technology consulting with customers across many industries and geographies. In his free time, he enjoys running and playing with his dog Nala. Paul Hargis Paul has focused his efforts on machine learning at several companies, including AWS, Amazon, and Hortonworks. He enjoys building technology solutions and teaching people how to use them. Paul likes to help customers expand their machine learning initiatives to solve real-world problems. Prior to his role at AWS, he was lead architect for Amazon Exports and Expansions, helping

items.title: Amazon SageMaker JumpStart: 2026 year-to-date in review
items.description: Amazon SageMaker JumpStart is a machine learning (ML) hub within Amazon SageMaker AI that provides access to a curated catalog of AI models, solution templates, and example notebooks. It reduces the time it takes to go from model selection to deployment. You can use it to evaluate open source large language models (LLMs), deploy a vision model for document understanding, or fine-tune a compact model on your own data. SageMaker JumpStart serves three primary use cases: Model discovery and evaluation — Browse hundreds of foundation models (FMs) from providers like Alibaba (Qwen), NVIDIA, Google, Mistral, Cohere, IBM, and more. Each model card includes architecture details, benchmarks, licensing information, and sample notebooks. One-click deployment — Deploy your choice of model to a SageMaker real-time inference endpoint with pre-configured settings optimized for your workload (low cost, low latency, throughput, or balanced). No manual container or instance configuration required. Model customization — Fine-tune models directly from the console or SDK using techniques like low-rank adaptation (LoRA), supervised fine-tuning (SFT), direct preference optimization (DPO), and reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR). Serverless customization options reduce infrastructure management. You can access SageMaker JumpStart through the SageMaker Studio console (Models → JumpStart models), programmatically through the SageMaker Python SDK, or directly from Hugging Face using the recently launched deep link integration. 2026 onboarding at a glance From January through September 2026, SageMaker JumpStart onboarded over 100 new models across 30 distinct providers. This represents a significant expansion of the catalog, driven by the accelerating pace of open source model releases and growing customer demand for choice across model architectures, sizes, and capabilities. Here’s a breakdown of the leading contributors and a link to our SageMaker JumpStart page : Alibaba (Qwen): 29 models spanning reasoning (Qwen 3.8-27B), large-scale mixture-of-experts (Qwen3.5-122B-A10B), agentic workflows (Qwen-AgentWorld-35B-A3B), code generation (Qwen3-Coder-Next, Qwen 3 Coder 30B), speech recognition (Qwen3-ASR-1.7B), text-to-speech (Qwen3-TTS), embeddings (Qwen3-VL-Embedding-2B), and reranking (Qwen3-Reranker-4B). NVIDIA: 17 models including the Cosmos3 world foundation model family (Super, Edge, Nano), Cosmos Reason 7B, MSA-Search, Nemotron 3.5 Lightning , Nemotron-3-Super-120B (FP8 and BF16), Nemotron3 Ultra, Nemotron-Nano-12B-v2, Nemotron 3 Nano Omni (multimodal) , and Nemotron 3.5 Super VL for vision-language. Mistral: 7 models including the Ministral-3 family (3B, 8B, 14B in standard and BF16) and Voxtral-Mini-4B-Realtime for speech. Google: 6 Gemma 4 variants, including gemma-4-31B-it, E2B-it, E4B-it, 26B-A4B-it, assistant, and NVFP4 quantized. IBM: 4 models including Granite 4.0 h-micro/small/tiny and granite-speech-4.1-2b for multilingual automatic speech recognition (ASR) across 6 languages. Cohere: 4 models including Command A (A100) and Rerank v3.5, v4.0 Fast, and v4.0 Pro for retrieval augmentation. Others: 33 models from MiniMax, Zhipu AI (GLM), DeepSeek, Moonshot AI, Allen AI, Microsoft, Meta (Muse Spark) , Reflection (Beam) , Black Forest Labs, JetBrains, OpenBMB, BharatGenAI, Kakao, OpenFold, and more. Model onboarding highlights The models onboarded in 2026 reflect several focused priorities in how we expand the SageMaker JumpStart catalog. These aren’t only industry trends. They represent the areas where we see strong customer demand and significant opportunity to help customers build production AI applications on SageMaker. Expanding the NVIDIA open-model portfolio NVIDIA is one of our significant model providers, and in 2026 their contribution extended well beyond language models. The Cosmos3 world foundation models, available in Super, Edge, and Nano tiers, bring video generation, physics simulation, and action planning into a single architecture for physical AI applications such as robotics, autonomous systems, and digital twins. Combined with Nemotron models spanning from efficient edge inference (Nano-12B) to large-scale reasoning (Super-120B), SageMaker JumpStart now offers a broad portfolio of NVIDIA open models. If you build on NVIDIA hardware, you can deploy these models on SageMaker with optimized containers and pre-configured endpoints. Closing the multimodal gap Customer workloads increasingly require models that process more than text. In 2026, we prioritized onboarding models that handle vision, speech, and document understanding natively. NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Nano Omni processes text, vision, and speech in a single model. Google Gemma 4 adds vision-language capabilities across multiple sizes. IBM granite-speech-4.1-2b handles speech recognition and translation across six languages. Mistral Voxtral-Mini supports real-time speech understanding. These additions mean customers can avoid chaining separate preprocessing models for multimodal workloads. Making creative AI accessible Image and video generation moved from niche to mainstream in 2026. We onboarded FLUX.2 Small Decoder and FLUX.2-klein-base-4B from Black Forest Labs for fast text-to-image generation, Meta Muse-Glimmer-30B for multimodal agentic workflows, and NVIDIA Cosmos3 for video generation. With these models, you can access creative AI capabilities with the same one-click deployment experience you use for language models. Prioritizing efficient and quantized models Not every workload requires a frontier-scale model, and many customers are focused on optimizing inference costs as they move to production. We onboarded multiple quantized and compact models: Zhipu AI GLM-5.2 FP8 delivers strong performance with a reduced memory footprint. items.title: Accused OpenAI spy had folder called “Saudi Gov Docs,” FBI says
items.description: On Monday, a court granted the US government's request to deny release of a former OpenAI engineer accused of bugging a top-secret conference room to steal the frontier lab’s secrets. In a court filing Sunday, US attorney Craig Missakian argued that Abdulrahman Alfozan must continue to be detained while the US makes its case that Alfozan brazenly spied on OpenAI, either for his own personal business gain or to benefit the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia. Evidence showed that Alfozan had been chatting with a member of the KSA royal family on WhatsApp, while pursuing opportunities to permanently move back to Saudi Arabia during the country's biggest AI push yet, the government argued. Shortly before his arrest, the FBI found he accessed a folder called "Saudi Gov Docs" on his iPhone, where he also allegedly stored photos of a second bug he planted in the offices.
