items.title: Germany Wants to Lead the World in Industrial AI: How NVIDIA Will Help
items.description: In the cavernous hall of Kraftwerk, a former power station in Berlin, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and NVIDIA founder and CEO Jensen Huang sat down to discuss Germany’s AI roadmap, and in particular, the industrial applications of AI. Huang opened by tracing NVIDIA’s longstanding relationship with German industry, beginning with gaming systems, workstations and automotive design in the early 2000s and leading to today’s partnerships in autonomous vehicle development and digital twins for manufacturing. The conversation focused on how Germany can make the most of the AI revolution by playing to its strengths in manufacturing and automotive — and by encouraging AI adoption across the country’s ecosystem of small and medium-sized companies. Read All NVIDIA in Europe Announcements Earlier in the day, as part of the Invest in Germany Summit, Chancellor Merz, the Federal Ministry for Economic Affairs and Energy and the Federal Ministry for Research, Technology and Space signed a Joint Declaration of Intent with NVIDIA. The German federal government’s aim is to merge traditional German engineering and manufacturing expertise with cutting-edge research and AI technology. The declaration sets out an agreement to work on a joint initiative with NVIDIA to advance cutting edge AI models for physical AI. Formalizing and expanding NVIDIA’s collaboration with Germany’s federal government and its “Industry 4.0 Platform,” which is comprised of representatives from politics, industry, research and trade associations, helps achieve the government’s stated goal to “systematically bring industrial AI into widespread use and to establish a state-of-the-art industrial AI ecosystem in Europe.” Germany’s Ambition to Integrate AI With Industry Merz and Huang dug into industrial AI and how NVIDIA can help Germany lead the way. The German Chancellor first laid out his government’s ambition. “We are fully committed to be one of the most advanced places in the world, not just in the European Union, but in the world to work with AI, to integrate AI into our industry,” Merz said. “I’m really optimistic that we will be one of the leading, if not the leading, country in the world in terms of the spread of AI for all the companies — our manufacturers, machinery, automotive industry and suppliers of the automotive industry. I think this is a great opportunity.” Merz called out the leaders of the small and medium businesses — the Mittelstand — in the audience. “The biggest advantage we have in Germany is our so-called Mittelstand,” Merz said. “Please open your doors for AI to make use of your data. This is a real secret and a real advantage for Germany to make use of all the data which is already available in our companies.” Huang agreed, and praised Germany’s world-class expertise in manufacturing companies both large and small, as well as its math and science excellence. That national expertise and knowledge is what sets the German economy apart, he said, and AI will only amplify it. “That knowledge belongs to you,” Huang said. “It cannot be replaced. AI can only augment your capability, it will not replace your capability. Take advantage of the technology. It’s a new instrument.” Germany’s expertise with physical technologies is a differentiator, Huang and Merz agreed, and a powerful accelerator for the German economy when AI is included. “If we are successful in bringing these two aspects and parts of the business of the future together,” Merz said. “I’m really very optimistic that Germany can be one of the most successful economies in the world.” Huang described AI’s impact across virtually every industry as a new industrial revolution. “This industrial revolution is so mighty, so powerful,” Huang said. “In the Chancellor’s words, you are re-engineering Germany. This is your chance to do it well.” Merz envisioned a regular reunion with Huang to assess the progress Germany is making with AI. “I would like to see him regularly, let’s say at least once a year, and discuss the progress we made,” Merz said, “And see a guy sitting in my office being extremely happy about Germany as a place to invest.” NVIDIA’s Investments in Germany Huang also announced new investments in four German startups, part of a nearly $10 billion commitment by NVIDIA to support companies, universities, research institutions and more across Europe. NVIDIA has been investing across Germany’s startup ecosystem, supporting leading technology companies including n8n, Neura Robotics and Black Forest Labs . Today, Huang announced new planned investments in Agile Robots, Avelios Medical, Mirelo and Reflex Aerospace. Agile Robots, a Munich-based robotics company, builds AI-powered robots, from robotic arms to its Agile ONE humanoid, for manufacturing, logistics and healthcare. Avelios Medical, a Munich-based healthcare technology startup, develops an AI-native hospital information system that serves as the core system of record for clinical and administrative workflows, integrating AI directly into hospital operations to free up doctors and nurses to deliver better patient care. Mirelo , a German startup, develops AI models that generate sound effects, speech and music for video, helping creators and production teams produce high-quality audio that perfectly matches their visuals on screen. Reflex Aerospace, a Berlin-based space scaleup, designs and builds high-performance satellites ready for launch in about 12 months instead of years. Siemens and NVIDIA Advance Autonomous Manufacturing; Record-Breaking Quantum Simulation Earlier in the day, Siemens announced it’s partnering with NVIDIA to advance AI-driven, autonomous factories. Siemens showcased new AI solutions at its Erlangen factory , advancing its role as a global blueprint for autonomous manufacturing. Fully virtual production ramp-up reduces engineering effort by up to 85%, while agent-based production planning enables more adaptive manufacturing and cost savings of up to 20%. NVIDIA researchers

items.title: Cutting our inference bill by 68% by being obsessive about optimization
items.description: When we previously blogged about our AI code reviewer in April , an average review cost a palatable $1.19. By the end of August, that figure had shot up to about $2.46. We hadn't made any significant architectural changes: the coordinator was still handing work to the same set of specialist reviewers, and the same risk tiers decided how intensive of a review we gave. Around mid-September we tasked our agents with working out where those tokens were going and cutting them — aggressively. With code quality at high effort, the average review now costs just $0.77, down 68% from the $2.43 it averaged over our two most expensive weeks before we started. Our main goal was to cut costs, but as part of this work we also managed to optimize the reviewer, so that the median review now takes just 1m 32s instead of the 4m 09s it took before. About 40% of the savings came from changes and optimizations to the reviewer's code, and the rest from experimenting with which models we use and how much effort they put in. How a review doubled in cost The chart below shows the cost of an average review on each weekday since March. It holds the mix of review tiers fixed, so a day with more large reviews doesn't skew the data. The cost per review steadily rose from $1.22 (March) → $1.44 (June) → $1.74 (July) and finally, to $2.32 (August). A small part of that is that more reviews landed in the most expensive tier (59% of reviews in March and then 65% in August). We believe there’s a simple answer for why: models are getting much better, and much more capable. Naturally, engineers are producing bigger, more complex changes which means more of them fall into our “full review” tier. We found that most of the cost increase actually came from model changes over those months, though. At the start of August we moved every reviewer onto Anthropic models, which raised the cost per job from $1.38 to $2.03. We made this choice because we found that during our evals, Anthropic models performed better on this specific workload than other models. Our internal standards reviewer, Codex , ended up on Claude Opus 4.7 due to a mix of performance and reliability. That took it from about $0.25 per review to $0.88 in August, which made it more expensive than the coordinator agent itself. The cache hit rate also increased, going from 85.7% in April to 97% by September, while the number of tokens per review more than tripled, from 0.91 million to 2.99 million. A high hit rate on three times as many tokens still costs a lot more, even with the low cache read cost. What else has changed since our last post? One of the biggest changes is that the reviewer now runs on OpenCode v2, which is a ground-up rewrite from v1. Before switching all reviews over from v1 to v2, we ran every review in every canary repo on both v1 and v2 in a comparative shadow mode. The two agreed on the approval decision in 98% of the merge requests we tested, so we moved everyone over in one go in early October and removed the v1 code. Comparing two days with the same models, full-tier reviews on v2 finish about 13% faster. We’re also currently experimenting with other ways to run our internal AI reviewer, including solely on Durable Objects using pi-durable . We’re hopefully going to have more on this coming soon, so keep an eye out! So, where were the tokens going? Right before we started focusing on cost optimization, our AI review spend was split by: output tokens making up about 23%, cache writes cost 43%, and cache reads cost 34%. This means that most of the money was going on context the model had already seen or was about to see again. That makes complete sense when you look into a single session. The code quality reviewer made 16.6 large language model (LLM) calls per review on average and over those calls it wrote 72k tokens to the cache and read back 1.08m, because each call sends the whole conversation as context. A session's cost grows with both the number of calls and the size of the context, and over the last few months we had slowly increased both. It’s worth taking a few minutes to read about how Anthropic's prompt cache works. It works by caching parts of the prompt that have already been computed by the large language model (LLM). These are known as prefixes, because they only work on the messages at the start of the conversation, not mid way through or the end. This means that a future request can reuse an earlier prefix, up to the part of the conversation that changes from what’s been cached. In our case, the harness tools, system prompt and messages at the start of our AI reviewer sessions rarely change, so they’re a great candidate for prefix caching. A prefix is only stored where a cache breakpoint ends it. Writing to the cache costs 1.25 times the normal input price and reading costs 0.1 times, and an entry expires after five minutes unless something reads it. That means we had two things to work on: make the first request of each session read from the cache instead of writing to it, and make each session use fewer calls. Sharing a cached prefix between every repository Beginning September 14, the reviewer recorded the token usage of each reviewer's first LLM call, plus a hash of the first system block exactly as it was sent to the provider. The data showed that the first request of a session found a cached prefix only 14% to 26% of the time. Every session starts with the same tool definitions and the same agent prompt, between 11k and 21k tokens that are identical in every repository we review, so almost all of them should have been cache hits. The problem ended up being in how OpenCode v1 constructed the system prompt: It built one block containing our agent prompt, followed by an environment section with the working directory and the date, and placed the only cache breakpoint at the end of that block. items.title: How to continue a GitHub Copilot app session in VS Code
items.description: The agent has finished the bulk of your change. Now you want to inspect one implementation detail, adjust a few lines by hand, and run the project locally before you ship it. But the work is sitting in the GitHub Copilot app … and your editor is where you review diffs, debug code, and make final adjustments. Do you have to choose between staying in the session and starting over in Visual Studio Code? You don’t. You can open the Copilot app session directly in VS Code and continue with its conversation, code changes, and working context intact. That means Copilot can handle the repetitive or time-consuming work, then hand control back to you for closer review, hands-on editing, and local testing. In this tutorial, you’ll learn how to: Open a Copilot app session in VS Code. Review the agent’s changes line by line. Continue the same conversation from your editor. Modify and test the code locally. Push your updates to the pull request associated with the session. Prerequisites Before you begin, make sure you have: The GitHub Copilot app installed and signed in. Visual Studio Code installed and connected to the same GitHub account. A Copilot app session with code changes you want to review or continue. Permission to work in and push changes to the session’s repository. This tutorial assumes you are already comfortable navigating VS Code, running commands in its integrated terminal, and working with Git branches and pull requests. 1. Start with a session in the Copilot app Open the session you want to continue. Before handing it off, take a moment to review the task and the work Copilot completed. A session contains more than a collection of modified files. It also records the task, the plan, and the conversation that produced those changes. That context is important when you want to understand why Copilot chose a particular implementation or ask it to revise part of the work. You do not need to summarize that history or copy it into a new chat before moving to VS Code. 2. Open the session in VS Code From the session, select Open in VS Code . If the app presents more than one supported editor or VS Code installation, choose the one you want to use. VS Code opens the project using the worktree associated with the session. It also displays the existing session in the Copilot sidebar. That gives you three connected pieces of the original work: The session context: The task, plan, and conversation remain available. The diff: The files and lines changed by the agent are ready for review. The worktree: VS Code opens the same isolated working tree the session used. You are continuing the existing session, not reconstructing it in a new editor window. 3. Review the agent’s changes Before editing, inspect the diff in VS Code. Open the Source Control view to see the changed files, then select a file to review its changes line by line. Review the implementation as you would any other proposed change. In particular, check that: The code solves the requested problem. The implementation follows the repository’s conventions. Error states and edge cases are handled appropriately. Tests cover the behavior that changed. No unrelated files or behaviors were modified. The preserved conversation can help explain how Copilot arrived at the implementation. If something is unclear, continue prompting Copilot in the sidebar. For example: Explain why you changed this function instead of adding a new helper. Identify any behavior this could affect. You can also ask Copilot to make another change. Because the session and worktree remain connected, you do not have to describe the task from the beginning. 4. Make a hands-on edit Once you understand the proposed changes, edit any file directly in VS Code. This is useful for adjustments that are faster or easier to make by hand, such as: Refining a label or error message. Renaming a variable for clarity. Adjusting layout or styling. Adding a missing test case. Applying a repository-specific convention. You are editing the session’s existing worktree, so your manual changes build directly on the agent’s work. You do not need to copy files between directories or manually re-create the branch. 5. Run and verify the project locally Use the VS Code integrated terminal to run the project’s normal validation workflow. The exact commands depend on the repository, but some web app examples may include: npm install npm test npm run lint npm run dev Treat agent-generated changes the same way you would treat code written by a person: run the relevant tests, inspect failures, and verify the behavior yourself. If the development server prints a localhost URL, open it to test the change in a browser. When supported by your VS Code setup, you can open the URL in VS Code’s integrated browser and inspect the result without leaving the editor. For a user-interface change, verify both the requested behavior and nearby states. For example, check the modified component at different viewport sizes and confirm that loading, empty, and error states still work. 6. Continue with Copilot or keep editing yourself At any point, you can choose the interaction that best fits the next step: Prompt Copilot when the change requires repository-wide analysis or repetitive edits. Edit directly when you know the exact change you want. Use both approaches iteratively as you test and refine the implementation. For example, after making a manual UI adjustment, you might ask Copilot: Add a test for the updated label and run the relevant test file. Do not modify unrelated components. Because you are still in the original session, Copilot retains the context needed to interpret “the updated label.” 7. Commit and push the finished changes When the implementation is ready, review the final diff one more time. Then commit and push the changes using the Source Control view or the integrated terminal: git status git add git commit -m "Refine sess

items.title: Making the internet better for AI agents might make it worse for everyone else
items.description: This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here . Until recently, you could divide internet users into just two categories: bots and people. Websites have long allowed bots to perform automated tasks, like capturing the content of web pages, but rules govern what they can access and how they behave. The web, after all, is designed primarily for people, even if we occasionally have to solve puzzles and captchas to prove we are not bots. But this is being entirely upended by the release of personal AI agents, which can do things for you online, like booking flights or hotel rooms. They have recently been unleashed at scale by the launch of apps like OpenAI’s Dots and Meta’s Muse. Muse was downloaded 5 million times in its first month, and agentic web traffic tripled from August to September. The mingling of these agents with human visitors—on an internet designed largely to prioritize people—has gone poorly, with many websites blocking AI agents that consumers have sent to negotiate prices or plan vacations. Still, if the demand for agents keeps going up, the internet will be increasingly redesigned for them instead of us. Such changes are coming because agents really do mark a third category of web visitor. They’re not humans, of course, and they use the internet at machine speed. But they’re not quite bots, either, because they’re acting on behalf of individual people to do tasks that can be perfectly legitimate and useful. They just work faster than a person would. Since agents don’t fit into the systems we have for differentiating bots from people, some platforms (especially the more security-conscious ones) have opted to just ban them entirely. TechCrunch recently reported people having trouble deploying their agents to websites ranging from Pizza Hut to Yelp, which doesn’t allow AI to book restaurant reservations. Amazon has blocked Muse’s agents and is waging a court battle against the AI startup Perplexity to block its agents too. Though a judge recently ruled in favor of Perplexity, Amazon has filed an appeal in which it argues that AI agents threaten its advertising business by making it harder to distinguish between ads seen by humans and those served to bots. These blocks are annoying for early adopters, but Ethan Mollick, an associate professor at the Wharton School of the University of Pennsylvania, predicts it will soon affect the whole web. Once it becomes common knowledge that AI agents can be sent to request refunds or negotiate prices, for example, agents will overwhelm customer service departments to the point where they become unusable by real people. “Humans will eventually get very annoyed when their agents aren’t allowed to do this on their behalf,” he recently wrote on LinkedIn. If demand for personal agents grows, platforms will find ways to let them in. That’s especially true because the vast majority of agentic web traffic is to e-commerce sites, meaning that platforms have money to be made if they allow the legions of new AI agents to shop on behalf of real people. Indeed, the e-commerce giant Shopify is already welcoming the agents by giving them their own checkout lanes that bypass pages designed for humans. The pressing question is what will happen to the internet for the rest of us in the process. We’ve grown used to a web where, even as it’s increasingly designed to exploit our attention, humans have at least remained the intended users. But that internet might yield to one optimized instead for the agents that will eventually outnumber us, making it even more miserable for the humans who are left. How might this go? Perhaps websites become increasingly neglected as destinations for real people. Humans who want to browse and compare products themselves encounter worse interfaces. Verification systems are imperfect; imagine constantly being asked to verify that you’re a human, not an agent (and hey, maybe you’ll need to get your iris scanned to do so). That sweater you want doesn’t have one price listed for everyone but instead displays different prices to different people’s agents. You can never tell when your agent’s recommendation is influenced by advertisements or platform commissions. That’s a far cry from the future promised by Google , Anthropic , and OpenAI , in which AI agents will give consumers greater power and bargaining leverage. But that promise is not outlandish. Agents are capable of genuinely helping people by fighting bogus medical bills or researching more affordable car insurance, for example. Whether they can actually be used for these purposes depends on what rules are set for how agents interact with websites and what exactly they’re allowed to do. These rules are still being written. Some of them will benefit all of us—neither consumers nor businesses want credit card information to be waved around by agents wherever they roam the web, for example, and rules to keep agents more secure are a good thing. It’s the more contested ones, like whether businesses can block agents from their websites or prevent them from negotiating better deals for consumers, that will determine whether the web becomes a highway for agents working for us or against us.

items.title: Introducing Clairic, a new System One class of extraction models
items.description: Today, we're announcing a preview of a new class of System One-style models: extraction models. Our first one, Clairic, is available hosted on Workers AI as @cf/cloudflare/clairic. We intend to release the model open-weights soon. Clairic is an extraction model that is able to extract, compute, estimate, and forecast values from unstructured inputs — all at a significantly higher accuracy, faster latency, and cheaper cost than traditional LLMs. Context When System One models were announced by TypeSafe a month ago, it took the industry by storm. As referenced by TypeSafe in their blog and defined by Daniel Kahneman’s book Thinking, Fast and Slow , a System One model should be fast and precise, which contrasts a System Two model that is capable of deliberate reasoning (like LLMs). With this, TypeSafe introduced Jev — a model that is purpose-fit for a specific use case, and priced accessibly given its niche domain. It excelled where LLMs failed, helping users make decisions based on probabilities and well-typed outputs. The introduction of Jev prompted people to start thinking about a new class of models that were not LLMs and how to integrate them into their workflows. We were inspired by the concept of System One models and started thinking about other tasks where LLMs are inefficient. There are many structured-output calls going to frontier LLMs today with the same shapes again and again: What's the invoice total? When was this delivered? How many days late is it? What will this repair cost? What will traffic look like over the next 24 hours? None of these have answers you can list out in advance, which is needed for a decision model to give probabilities against. That led us to the class of models we're introducing today: System One extraction models. Introducing System One extraction models Until now, every System One model has been a decision model: Jev and Clef take an input state and a list of questions and give probabilities against the inputs and your listed questions. Clairic is the first model in a new class: System One extraction models. It is still fast, typed, and cheap, but it answers with values directly extracted from the input, computed from it, or predicted beyond it. Most model tasks ask for one of three kinds of output: a number, a choice from a fixed set, or open-ended text. Clairic handles the first, returning numbers with an 80% range, and also pulls typed values like names, dates and lists out of the input. Clef handles the second: it picks among options and returns a probability for each. LLMs handle the third. We call Clairic and Clef System One models because they answer in a single pass, without reasoning or generating tokens. They charge only for input and typically respond in under a second, while an LLM that reasons through the same step takes several seconds. An extraction model can return: Extracted values: Text copied from the input, such as a name, an order ID or a description. Each one comes back as a span with its character offsets and a confidence score. Including, computed values: Numbers, dates, times, datetimes, durations and lists, read from the input or worked out from it. They follow the rules of their type (for example, two decimals for cents) and come with a confidence score. Estimated values: Values the input doesn't state but gives evidence for. Each one comes back as a distribution inside the bounds you declare, on the grid you specify, with a median and an 80% interval. Forecasted values: Future values of a series, one estimate per step ahead, each with its own 80% interval. And because it generates no tokens, it can't produce a mistyped answer or “hallucinate” in the same way as an LLM (though it can, of course, make mistakes). Outputs are a value of the type you asked for, or null when the model fails to find an answer in the input. It also comes with confidence scores against the outputs to help you evaluate if it is appropriate to trust the model or to take a second look. Here’s how extraction models fit into the landscape of System One and System Two models: System One: Extract System One: Decide System Two Example models Clairic Jev, Clef GPT, Claude, Gemini, DeepSeek Sampling One parallel pass One parallel pass One token at a time Purpose Predict values Make decisions Write and reason ML framing Regression and extraction Classification Generation Thinking mode System 1: fast, one pass System 1: fast, one pass System 2: slow, deliberate Output Typed values: spans, numbers, dates, times, lists, distributions, with calibrated probabilities Typed decisions: options with calibrated probabilities Free-form strings Output space Continuous, but typed and bounded by your schema A finite set of options you list Anything What it answers What's the amount? When does it happen? How much will it be? Which category is it? Is it legitimate? Which action should we take? Why did it happen? How should we approach it? Can you fix it? Output always a valid response? Yes: every answer is a value of its declared type (or null), inside your bounds Yes: answers are always one of your options No: strings must be parsed and checked Together, these models can work together in unison to help you get closer to parsing through real-world data, making decisions on inputs, and then taking actions. Extraction models turn raw input into typed values, decision models turn values into decisions, and LLMs turn decisions into words. How a request works Clairic is designed differently than an LLM. Similar to a decision model, it only processes input tokens with a single forward pass, and thus has no charge for output tokens. It is much faster, cheaper, and more accurate than an LLM for certain use cases. A request is a state (the text to read, plus up to four optional images) and a map of typed fields . You name each field, give it a type and optional plain-language instructions , and get back one typed answer per field, all from one parallel

items.title: “We were looking at it wrong”: The explosive claim that’s upended the AI world
items.description: “I think I have good news about the nature of neural networks.” With those simple words of optimism, Nick Cammarata, a researcher at the AI startup Goodfire, kicked off a 26,000-word blog post that has knocked the AI world on its head, sparking wild speculation as well as cautious (and not-so-cautious) celebration. Cammarata’s claim is that LLMs might in fact be far easier to understand—and thus to monitor and control—than people previously thought. If true (and we’ll come back to that), it’s a huge deal. After a summer filled with revelations that swarms of agents built by top firms like OpenAI and Anthropic have been breaking their containment and causing havoc on the public internet—often while those companies weren’t aware of what their agents were up to—the AI industry is desperate to get a better handle on the technology it has built. That’s one reason the blog post landed with such force. “I think this may be remembered as a major moment in scientific history,” one AI researcher posted on X : “I feel like my understanding of what a neural net is has been catapulted into the future by five years or something.” Another called it “the most important AI paper of the year.” Not everyone is convinced, however. What Cammarata has shared is little more than a hunch, says Chris Potts at Stanford University, who leads a team that is trying to understand how LLMs work. “As far as I can tell, nothing about this blog post makes the problems any easier,” he says. “It would not have occurred to me to say this at all, but very prominent people on social media seem to believe that it is an all-encompassing breakthrough.” I talked to Cammarata the day after his post blew up. He says he was surprised by the response: “I didn’t expect people to update [their beliefs about AI] quite as much as they did.” “I just really enjoy looking at neural networks,” he says. “Honestly, I really like doing this stuff. And after looking a lot, I have a hopeful story.” Knotted networks It has long been accepted that the mechanisms inside neural networks, the software that underpins most AI models, are very hard—perhaps impossible—to unpick fully. That’s because when the networks are trained, they appear to take on weird, tangled structures that make no sense to a human. Researchers like to say today’s AI is grown like a garden, not built like a bridge. Cammarata has done more than most to establish that view. He previously worked at OpenAI, where he helped pioneer techniques that allowed researchers to peer inside models, including tools that can probe individual neurons to see what they represent. It’s a little like how neuroscientists use MRI to study brains. ( MIT Technology Review chose this approach, known as mechanistic interpretability, as one of its 10 hottest technologies of 2025 .) Back in 2020, Cammarata and a few colleagues were studying a small image-recognition model called Inception v1. (The work was led by Chris Olah, who went on to cofound Anthropic, where he now leads the firm’s interpretability research.) When they looked at its neurons, it seemed to be using them to capture multiple things at once. For example, they found that one neuron responded to both images of cars and images of cats. The researchers concluded that the model was getting at least some of its neurons to multitask, perhaps so that it could fit in more data. Other researchers, looking at other models, backed this up . The phenomenon became known as superposition: Models folded unrelated concepts into single neurons. The upshot was clear: When you looked inside a model, what you saw was a vast, tangled knot. Most mechanistic interpretability research has therefore focused on ways to untangle that knot . But despite a few breakthroughs , progress has been slow. Today’s models, such as the latest LLMs, are so large and complex that researchers can make sense of only tiny pieces at a time. Some leading figures in the field doubt if it will ever be possible to understand an LLM in fine-grained detail . Cammarata was one of them. “I was very pessimistic,” he says. But then he took the trouble to really look. Nothing but neurons At Goodfire, Cammarata spends nearly all of his time peering inside neural networks. He has built new tools and deploys teams of AI agents to help him make sense of what he sees. “I spent like, I don’t know, 10 hours a day, seven days a week, for most of the last year just looking at neurons,” he says. What he claims to have realized is that there is a kind of logic to neural networks after all, even if they seem to make no sense at first. “We were looking at it wrong,” he says. “I just think you want to try slightly harder; you don’t want to give up too quickly.” Cammarata almost makes it sound like a conversion of faith. Those early experiments with models such as Inception v1, which suggested that neural networks were tangled up, fostered a kind of confirmation bias. When researchers looked at a new model, they expected to be flummoxed, he says. “Every time I couldn’t understand something, I was like, ‘Wow, this untangling process is even more important than I thought, because I can’t make any progress without it.’” But the more Cammarata looked at neurons, he says, the more things started to fall into place. “Not all of them are flawless, but I expected nothing to be legible, or very little to be legible,” he says. “And actually, I was able to, like, map out whole circuitry.” Back to cars and cats Cammarata took his new approach—and his new agents—and went back to Inception v1. “I’d studied that for probably thousands of hours,” he says. But with fresh eyes, Cammarata found things that he now thinks they got wrong the first time around. Take the car-and-cat neuron. Rather than asking why multiple unrelated things were packed into a single neuron, he now tried to figure out what those things might have in common. It hit him: It was a V shape. “I was looking at the same images; there was no technical change,”

items.title: AI game clones are making indie developers afraid to show their work
items.description: Since its earliest days, the video game industry has been built on developers creating clones of competing games , with varying levels of originality and varying levels of enforcement from game platforms . Now, though, AI coding tools are making that cloning process so efficient that many developers are getting extremely cautious about sharing their early work too widely. Developer Alliance Arts highlighted this trend over the weekend, delaying the launch of a planned public demo for its demon-themed Russian Roulette drinking game Drunken Goddess Reflux , which had been set to go live with today's launch of Steam Next Fest . In a post on social media Friday evening , the Alliance Arts team wrote that, in addition to concerns about managing streaming restrictions, "we're concerned that the demo's content could be used to quickly imitate or replicate the game's presentation and gameplay with AI or other tools and that such works could be released before our launch." items.title: Pegasus 1.5 from TwelveLabs is now available in Amazon Bedrock
items.description: On Oct 9, 2026 we announced the availability of TwelveLabs’ Pegasus 1.5 on Amazon Bedrock . Pegasus 1.5 is a video language model that turns long-form video into structured, timestamped metadata. You describe the moments that matter to your workflow, and the model returns every matching segment as JSON. Video represents a significant and complex category of unstructured data, yet most of it remains unsearchable and underutilized. Extracting structured, actionable insights from that content has historically required labor-intensive manual review or fragmented toolchains. With earlier versions of Pegasus, you can point the model at a clip, ask a question, and get an answer. Now, Pegasus 1.5 analyzes the entire video, finds every segment that matches user-defined criteria, and returns structured, timestamped metadata. It also introduces video segmentation, multimodal prompting with reference images, and on-the-fly processing. With Pegasus 1.5 on Amazon Bedrock, you can analyze videos directly from an Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) URI or a base64 string with no pre-indexing required, and your data remains within the AWS data boundary. In this post, we cover what’s new in Pegasus 1.5, how the model is packaged on Amazon Bedrock, and how to send your first request. We then walk through video segmentation, structured JSON output, and multimodal prompting. What’s new in Pegasus 1.5 Pegasus 1.5 has the following changes compared to previous versions: Time-based metadata generation. You define the segments, events, or domain-specific cues that matter to your workflow, such as editorial segments, sports plays, speaker changes, or brand appearances. Pegasus 1.5 returns every matching segment as JSON, with start and end times and the requested fields populated. Multimodal prompting. A segment definition can combine a text description with a visual reference. This makes it possible to locate a specific product, logo, or person, along with what they are doing on screen. On-the-fly processing. No ingestion pipeline or pre-indexing step is required. Videos are sent directly from Amazon S3 and results are returned in the response. Extended processing capacity. Pegasus 1.5 analyzes videos up to two hours long in a single request, up from one hour in Pegasus 1.2. Pegasus 1.5 retains and enhances the core capabilities that made Pegasus 1.2 a powerful tool for video understanding, including: Video-to-text generation : Creates detailed textual descriptions based on video content. Granular visual comprehension : Analyzes objects, on-screen text, and numerical content within video frames. Temporal grounding : Accurately identifies timestamps of specific events within videos. Multimodal understanding : Combines visual, audio, and textual information for comprehensive analysis. Multilingual support : Full support for English, with partial support for Arabic, Chinese, French, German, Italian, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, Russian, Spanish, Thai, and Vietnamese. How Pegasus 1.5 works on Amazon Bedrock Pegasus 1.5 takes a video and either a text prompt or a set of segment definitions, and returns text or JSON. You call it on the bedrock-runtime endpoint with the InvokeModel API, or with InvokeModelWithResponseStream when you want the response streamed as it’s generated. Setting Value Model ID twelvelabs.pegasus-1-5-v1:0 AWS Region US West (Oregon), us-west-2 Inference On-demand APIs InvokeModel , InvokeModelWithResponseStream Each request runs in one of two analysis modes, chosen with the analysisMode field: Analysis mode analysisMode You send You get back General general (default) A text prompt in inputPrompt A text answer in message , or JSON when you supply a schema Time-based metadata time_based_metadata Segment definitions in responseFormat A segments list with start and end times and the fields you asked for You can point the model at video in two ways. An S3 location ( s3Location ) takes the object’s uri and the bucketOwner account ID, and suits long-form video. A base64 string ( base64String ) embeds the video in the request body, up to 25 MB, and suits short clips. To track cost by application, create an application inference profile from the Pegasus 1.5 model, tag it, and call it by its Amazon Resource Name (ARN) in place of the model ID. Getting started with Pegasus 1.5 The following section outlines how to get started with Pegasus 1.5. Prerequisites Before you begin, make sure you have: An active AWS account with Amazon Bedrock access. Python 3.10 or later, with the AWS SDK for Python (Boto3) installed. AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) permissions for bedrock:InvokeModel and bedrock:InvokeModelWithResponseStream . Model access enabled for TwelveLabs Pegasus 1.5 in the Amazon Bedrock console . Videos stored in an Amazon S3 bucket, or short clips you can send inline. The following policy grants both invoke actions on Pegasus 1.5. { "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Effect": "Allow", "Action": [ "bedrock:InvokeModel", "bedrock:InvokeModelWithResponseStream" ], "Resource": [ "arn:aws:bedrock:us-west-2::foundation-model/twelvelabs.pegasus-1-5-v1:0" ] } ] } Boto3 signs requests with your usual AWS credentials. You can also authenticate with an Amazon Bedrock API key by setting it in the AWS_BEARER_TOKEN_BEDROCK environment variable. For production, prefer a short-term key generated from your IAM credentials with the aws-bedrock-token-generator package, because it expires automatically. Bearer-token authentication also requires the bedrock:CallWithBearerToken permission. Send your first request Install Boto3: pip install boto3 The following example analyzes a video stored in Amazon S3 in general mode. This example uses the global Cross Region Inference (CRIS) endpoint. To target the US geographic endpoint instead, replace “global.” with “us.” in the endpoint URL. import boto3 import json from botocore.config import Config AWS_REGION = "us-west-2" MODEL_ID = "global.twelvelabs.pegasus

items.title: AIエージェントおすすめ17選！料金・無料枠・セキュリティを種類別に比較
items.description: AIエージェントを名乗るツールが増えすぎて、どれを選べばよいか迷っていませんか。本記事では、 法人で選ぶ価値のあるAIエージェント17選を、料金・無料で試せるか・学習利用の有無まで 2026年10月時点の公式情報で比較します。 ChatGPTやCopilotは使っているものの、Agentforce・Dify・Gensparkなどと何が違うのか、自社にはどれが合うのか判断がつかない。DX推進や情シスの担当者ほど、候補選びで手が止まりやすいでしょう。 2026年はAIエージェントの名称変更や料金改定が相次いでいます。半年前の比較記事をもとに稟議を出すと、 製品名や価格の誤りで差し戻される おそれがあります。 本記事では、おすすめの17ツールを汎用型・業務システム搭載型・業務特化型・ノーコード型・開発支援型に分けて紹介し、社内で使っているシステム別の早見表と、無料トライアルで見極める手順を解説します。 読み終えるころには、自社に合う候補を2〜3個に絞り込み、料金とセキュリティの根拠をそろえてトライアルに進める状態になります。まずは比較の視点から確認していきましょう。 おすすめのAIエージェントを比較する4つの視点 おすすめのAIエージェントを比べるときは、以下の4つの視点を押さえます。 提供形態は自社の業務に合うか 料金体系は予算を組みやすいか 無料で試せるか 法人向けのセキュリティは十分か 4つの視点を先に決めておくと、後半の17選を読みながら候補を素早くふるい分けられます。 提供形態は自社の業務に合うか 最初に見るべきは、 そのAIエージェントがどの形で提供されているか です。 同じAIエージェントでも、ChatGPTのように単体で使う汎用型、Microsoft Copilotのように既存の業務システムに組み込まれた型、経理など特定業務に絞った型、自社で組み立てるノーコード型、開発専用の型では、得意な仕事がまったく異なります。 たとえば経費精算の不備チェックを任せたいなら、汎用型より経理特化型のほうが自社規程に沿った判定をすぐ始められます。 任せたい業務から逆算して型を決めると、17選のうち検討すべき候補が数個まで減り、比較にかける時間を短縮できます。 料金体系は予算を組みやすいか 料金は月額の金額だけでなく、 どの単位で課金されるか を確認します。 AIエージェントの課金方式は、1ユーザーあたりの定額、使った分だけのクレジット課金、ワークフローの実行回数課金などに分かれます。定額制は予算を組みやすい一方、クレジット制は利用が増えるほど請求額が膨らみます。 GitHub Copilotは2026年6月に全プランが従量課金へ移行するなど、課金方式そのものが変わる例もあります。 課金単位を把握しておけば、稟議書に「月額の上限」と「超過時の扱い」をセットで書けるため、経理や上長からの質問にもすぐ答えられます。 無料で試せるか 本契約の前に、 無料プランや無料トライアルで自社の業務を試せるか を確認しましょう。 AIエージェントは、デモで見た動きと自社データで動かしたときの精度に差が出やすいツールです。実際の業務で試さないまま契約すると、想定より修正の手間がかかるケースがあります。 ただし、無料プランがあってもエージェント機能は有料プラン限定という製品もあります。Claudeは無料プランを提供していますが、作業を任せるCoworkの機能は有料プランのみです。 「無料で何ができるか」まで確認しておくと、トライアル期間中に評価したい機能を確実に試せます。 法人向けのセキュリティは十分か 社内データを扱う以上、 入力した情報がAIの学習に使われない設定か は必ず確認します。 多くの製品は法人向けプランで学習利用を既定でオフにしていますが、個人向けプランでは扱いが異なる場合があります。あわせて、SSO（シングルサインオン）、SOC 2やISO 27001などの第三者認証、データの保存場所も比較の材料になります。 AIエージェントはメールやファイルを読み書きする権限を持つため、チャット型の生成AIより影響範囲が広くなります。 情シスやセキュリティ部門の審査項目を先に把握しておけば、候補選びの段階で審査に通りやすいツールへ絞れます。 おすすめのAIエージェント17選の比較一覧表 本記事で紹介する17ツールを、 種類・法人向け料金の目安・無料で試せるか・セキュリティ の4項目で一覧にしました。 ツール名 種類 法人向け料金の目安 無料で試せるか 学習利用・認証など ChatGPT 汎用型 Business：1ユーザー月20ドル〜 無料プランあり Business以上は学習利用なし・SOC 2 Claude 汎用型 Team Standard：1席月20ドル〜 無料プランはあるがCoworkは有料のみ Team以上は学習利用なし Gemini Enterprise 汎用型 Business：1席月21ドル〜 30日間の無料トライアル 学習利用なし Genspark 汎用型 Team：1席月40ドル〜 無料プランあり・機能制限あり Team以上は学習除外・SOC 2・ISO 27001 Microsoft Copilot 業務システム搭載型 Copilot Business：1ユーザー月3,148円〜 1か月の無料トライアル 学習利用なし・ISO 27001 Agentforce 業務システム搭載型 1ユーザー月600円＋利用クレジット Salesforce Foundationsで試用可 外部LLMはデータを保存・学習しない Notion AI 業務システム搭載型 Business：1メンバー月3,150円 Freeプランでお試し可 学習利用なし・SOC 2・ISMAP TOKIUM 業務特化型 業務量に応じた見積もり 一部エージェントを無料で試用可 ISMS・プライバシーマーク バクラク 業務特化型 要問い合わせ 要問い合わせ ISO 27001・SOC1 Type2 freee AIヘルプデスク 業務特化型 月5,000円〜 14日間の無料体験 AIの操作ログを記録 Sansan AIエージェント 業務特化型 要問い合わせ 要問い合わせ 公式発表に記載なし Copilot Studio ノーコード型 2万5,000クレジットで月29,985円 試用ライセンスあり・公開は不可 公式ページで要確認 Dify ノーコード型 Professional：年590ドル 無料プラン・オープンソース版あり SOC 2・ISO 27001 n8n ノーコード型 Starter：月20ユーロ〜 セルフホスト版は無料 SOC 2 GitHub Copilot 開発支援型 Business：1席月19ドル 無料プランあり・cloud agentは対象外 Business以上は学習利用なし OpenAI Codex 開発支援型 ChatGPTの各プランに含まれる ChatGPT無料プランで利用可 ChatGPT Business以上は学習利用なし Devin 開発支援型 Teams：1席月40ドル・最低月80ドル 無料プランあり 学習利用なし・SOC 2 ※2026年10月時点の各社公式サイトの表示額です。ドル・ユーロ建ては税別、円建ては各社の表示に準じます（Microsoftは税抜・年払い時の通常価格）。 料金はユーザー単位・クレジット単位・実行回数単位が混在しているため、単純な金額の大小では比べられません。気になるツールを見つけたら、次の種類別の解説で課金の仕組みまで確認してください。 幅広い業務に使える汎用型のおすすめAIエージェント4選 部署を問わず使える汎用型のおすすめAIエージェントは以下の4つです。 ChatGPT Claude Gemini Enterprise Genspark 全社で最初に1つ入れるなら、まずこの4つから候補を選ぶと失敗が少なくなります。 ChatGPT：社内アプリを横断して資料まで仕上げる OpenAIのChatGPTは、2026年7月に公開された ChatGPT Work でエージェント機能を提供しています。 ChatGPT Workは、複数のアプリをまたいで情報を集め、表・スライド・文書・Webアプリといった成果物まで仕上げます。時間のかかる作業も途中で止まらずに進められる点が特徴です。2025年に発表された「ChatGPT agent」は、現在このChatGPT Workに引き継がれています。 法人向けには、社内で共有できるクラウド上のエージェントを作れるworkspace agentsも、Business・Enterprise・Eduプランで提供されています。 Businessプランは1ユーザー月20ドル（年払い・2ユーザー以上、月払いは25ドル）で、業務データは既定で学習に使われません。日本国内でのデータ保存を選べるのはEnterpriseとEduのみです。 すでに社内でChatGPTが浸透している企業 なら、教育コストを抑えて導入できます。 > ChatGPTの料金ページはこちらから Claude：調査から文書作成まで任せられる AnthropicのClaudeは、 複数ステップの仕事を任せると完成した成果物で返してくれる 汎用型のAIエージェントです。 調査・文書作成・データ分析などをまとめて依頼でき、バックグラウンドで作業を進めます。もともと「Claude Cowork」という名称で提供されていた機能で、2026年9月にClaude本体へ統合されました。統合後の画面は個人向けのPro・Maxプランから順に提供されています。 法人向けのTeamプランは、Standardが1席月20ドル（年払い、月払いは25ドル）、Premiumが1席月100ドル（年払い、月払いは125ドル）です。Enterpriseは1席月20ドルに、API料金での従量課金が加わります（年払い・最低20席）。 Team・Enterpriseでは入力データが既定で学習に使われず、EnterpriseはSCIM・監査ログ・ISO 27001にも対応します。 長文の資料作成や調査レポートの比重が大きい部署 に向いています。 > Claudeの料金ページはこちらから Gemini Enterprise：Google Workspaceの情報を活用できる GoogleのGemini Enterpriseは、 社内のデータを横断して調べ、自社用のエージェントも作れる 法人向けのサービスです。 Gmail・ドキュメント・スプレッドシートなどGoogle Workspaceの情報をもとに回答でき、Deep Researchによる調査や、業務に合わせたカスタムエージェントの作成にも対応します。公式ページでは「Gemini for Business」という表記も使われています。 料金はBusinessエディションが1席月21ドルから、Standard・Plusエディションが1席月30ドルからです。Businessエディションには30日間の無料トライアルがあります。 入力データはモデルの学習に使われません。ただし、データの保存地域を指定できるのはStandard以上です。 Google Workspaceを全社で使っている企業 なら、既存のファイルをそのまま活用できます。 > Gemini Enterpriseの公式サイトはこちらから Genspark：調査とスライド作成を自動化できる Gensparkは、 Super Agentをはじめ複数のエージェントで調査から資料作成までを進められる 汎用型のサービスです。 Webでの情報収集、スライドや文書の作成など、リサーチ系の業務をまとめて任せられます。画面は日本語に対応しており、2026年1月には日本法人のGenspark株式会社が国内展開の強化を発表しました。 無料プランは1日100クレジットまで使えますが、AIモデルやエージェントの利用には制限があります。法人向けのTeamプランは1席月40ドル（年払いは35ドル）、Enterpriseは個別見積もりです。 Team以上はデータが学習から除外され、SAML SSO・SOC 2 Type II・ISO 27001に対応します。Enterpriseではデータの保存先に日本を選べるため、 国内保存を求められる企業 でも検討しやすいでしょう。 > Gensparkの法人プランはこちらから 業務システムに組み込まれたおすすめAIエージェント3選 普段使っている業務システムの中で動くおすすめAIエージェントは以下の3つです。 Microsoft Copilot Agentforce Notion AI すでに契約中のシステムであれば、新しいツールを覚える負担なく社員に使ってもらえます。 Microsoft Copilot：Word・Excel・PowerPointで作業を代行する Microsoft Copilotは、 Word・Excel・PowerPointの中で複数ステップの作業を代行する AIエージェントです。 2026年4月にWord・Excel・PowerPointのエージェント機能が正式提供となり、資料の下書きから表の分析、スライドの作成までをアプリ内で任せられます。調査用のResearcher、データ分析用のAnalystといったエージェントも標準で使えます。なお、製品名は「Microsoft 365 Copilot」から「Microsoft Copilot」へ変更されています。 中小企業向けのCopilot Businessアドオンは、1ユーザー月3,148円（税抜・年払い）です。2026年12月31日までのキャンペーンでは、年間契約の初年度が月2,698円になります。月払いは月3,778円で、1か月の無料トライアルも用意されています。 プロンプトや社内データは基盤モデルの学習に使われません。 Microsoft 365を全社導入している企業 にとって、最も導入しやすい選択肢でしょう。 > Microsoft Copilotの料金ページはこちらから Agentforce：Salesforce上で営業や顧客対応を自動化する SalesforceのAgentforceは、 Salesforce上の顧客データを使って営

items.title: How Deepgram optimized voice AI at scale with AWS Trainium
items.description: As voice becomes a first-class modality for AI, Deepgram’s models span speech-to-text, text-to-speech, and voice agents. They now process quadrillions of audio tokens a year for more than 200,000 developers and 1,400 organizations. Customers use them through the Deepgram API or run them in their own environments, including on Amazon SageMaker AI. For Deepgram, serving efficiency determines how much audio the system can process for a given infrastructure budget. High-volume batch workloads put heavy pressure on that budget, so the more efficiently each accelerator hour is used, the more audio Deepgram can serve on the same fleet. That made inference efficiency a natural target and Deepgram turned to AWS AI chips to improve it. They worked with AWS to bring its Nova-3 speech-to-text model to AWS Trainium2 for offline batch workloads such as contact-center analytics and medical transcription. The engagement began with Deepgram delivering Nova-3 as standard PyTorch code. Over several months, Deepgram and the AWS Forward Deployed Engineering (FDE) team ported Nova-3 to AWS Trainium2 in PyTorch reconstruction and tuned it for the new hardware. The final configuration runs eight model replicas on a single Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) trn2.3xlarge instance. On Deepgram’s offline, throughput-oriented batch workloads, that setup processed 11–70 percent more audio per dollar than the compute options Deepgram had been running. We measured this using instance pricing at the time of the evaluation. These gains help Deepgram scale efficiently, keep shipping better models, and bring them to customers at lower prices. These benefits can extend to customers who self-host Deepgram models in their own virtual private cloud (VPC) on Amazon SageMaker AI. There, Deepgram and AWS continue to improve ease of setup, reliability, and observability. In this post, we walk through the full inference optimization effort on Trainium: porting Nova-3 to the AWS Neuron software stack, the kernel-level tuning that followed, the data-parallel Rust runtime that lets Deepgram’s own model server call Trainium, and the throughput and cost results we measured on batch transcription. Optimizing Nova-3 to Trainium2 with native PyTorch Starting with standard PyTorch code, we used TorchNeuron, the native PyTorch integration of the Neuron Compiler, which supports both eager execution and torch.compile . We ran Nova-3 in eager mode on Trainium2 first and checked which operations fell back to the CPU, then compiled with torch.compile . The compiled path ran every model operation on Trainium2 with no CPU fallbacks detected. We compiled the encoder and decoder as separate static-shape graphs using torch.compile . Throughout, we checked numerical accuracy at two levels: layer-level output consistency against CPU, and the end-to-end Word Error Rate (WER), which had to stay in line with Deepgram’s reference values and target. From that working baseline, we kicked off the optimization work by replacing several layers with fused kernels from the public NKI Library (NKILib), a collection of pre-built reference kernels written with the Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI). The kernels covered operations such as fused QKV projections, fused feed-forward network (FFN) layers, and depthwise 1D convolution. We optimized for throughput and, by extension, cost efficiency, targeting Deepgram’s offline inference workloads. Throughput is reported as a relative gain over a baseline configuration rather than as absolute audio processed per second, and we swept batch sizes 1–128 to find the throughput-maximizing batch size. Kernel-level tuning with Neuron Explorer and NAD Enabling kernels is only the first step of an optimization flywheel: enable an NKI kernel (custom or from NKILib), profile the workload, then either tune the existing kernel or replace it with a new one based on the profiling insights. This cycle repeats until the performance target is met. At each step, a different part of the Neuron stack accelerates the work: NKILib provides drop-in replacement kernels, Neuron Explorer is the go-to tool for profiling Neuron workloads, and the Neuron Agentic Development (NAD) toolkit speeds up profiling analysis and kernel tuning through its profiling and kernel-writing skills. In our case, the NKILib kernels got us most of the way, and profiling showed where a hand-written kernel would do better. Each time, the NAD profiling skills took us from a Neuron Explorer profile to a root cause, and the NAD kernel-writing skills helped produce the replacement kernels. Layer What we found and changed Gain FFN The reference kernel’s tiling schedule reloaded the full set of projection weights from off-chip memory for every token tile, so memory bandwidth limited throughput as the token count grew. Our hand-tuned kernel loads each weight tile once, reuses it across multiple token tiles, and pipelines weight reads with on-chip compute. 2.0x lower latency compared to the reference kernel at batch size 96 Depthwise conv1d The experimental NKILib kernel framed the operation as an implicit general matrix multiply (GEMM), which left Tensor Engine utilization low. We rewrote it as a broadcast multiply-accumulate loop on the Vector Engine, reaching full engine utilization, enough to more than offset the Vector Engine’s lower peak throughput. 1.5x speedup compared to the reference kernel at batch size 96 Conv2d The model’s conv2d layers hit a compilation bottleneck: beyond batch size 32, these layers prevented the model from compiling as a single graph. Since NKILib had no conv2d kernel, we wrote one from scratch in NKI. The kernel went through several profiler-informed iterations following the flywheel described earlier, unlocking batch sizes above 32. Up to 50x on the convolution module at batch sizes ≤32 Data-parallel runtime in Rust Each Trainium2 device features eight physical NeuronCores, exposed by default as four logical NeuronCores (LNC2). items.description: AIエージェントの種類は、動作の仕組み・システム構成・用途・提供形態・自律性の5つの軸で整理できます。本記事では、 5つの軸ごとの種類と代表的なサービス を一覧で解説します。 Agentforce、Copilot Studio、Difyなど、AIエージェントを名乗るサービスが次々と登場しています。記事ごとに分け方が違い、どれがどの種類なのか整理できずに困っている方も多いでしょう。 種類の違いを押さえないまま選ぶと、目的に合わないツールでPoCを始め、時間と予算を無駄にします。反対に分類軸を理解すれば、社内で候補を説明し、比較の土台を作れます。 本記事では、5つの分類軸ごとのAIエージェントの種類と、 学術上の分類と実際のサービスの対応関係 を中心に解説します。 読み終えるころには、自社の業務に合う種類を絞り込み、試すべき候補を2〜3個に決められる状態になります。気になっているサービスを思い浮かべながら読み進めてください。 AIエージェントの種類は5つの分類軸で整理できる AIエージェントの種類は、 動作の仕組み・システム構成・用途・提供形態・自律性 の5つの軸で整理できます。各軸で決められることは以下のとおりです。 動作の仕組み：AIが何を手がかりに行動を決めるか システム構成：エージェントを1体で動かすか、複数で動かすか 用途：どの業務を任せるか 提供形態：どのような形で自社に導入するか 自律性：人の確認がどこまで必要か 分類軸 主な種類 この軸が役立つ場面 動作の仕組み 単純反射型・モデルベース反射型・目標ベース型・効用ベース型・学習 AIの判断力の水準を理解したいとき システム構成 シングルエージェント・マルチエージェント 複雑な業務をどう分担させるか考えるとき 用途 業務自動化型・情報検索型・カスタマー対応型など6種類 任せたい業務から候補を探すとき 提供形態 汎用型・業務システム搭載型・ノーコード開発型など5種類 導入方法と社内の体制を決めるとき 自律性 検索エージェント・タスクエージェント・自律エージェント 人の確認をどこに挟むか決めるとき ベンダー記事ごとに分け方が違うのは、それぞれが別の軸で語っているためです。自分が何を決めたいのかに合わせて軸を使い分けましょう。 AIエージェントは目標に向けて自律的に動くAI AIエージェントとは、与えられた目標に向けて、計画から実行までを自律的に進めるAIシステムです。AWSは、ユーザーに代わってタスクを推論・計画・完了するソフトウェアと説明しています。 出典： AI エージェント製品（AWS Marketplace） チャットのように1回ずつ指示を出さなくても、ゴールを伝えれば手順を自分で組み立てる点が特徴です。必要に応じて、Web検索や社内システムのAPIなど外部のツールも使います。 たとえば「来週の出張の候補便を調べ、条件に合う3便を表にまとめて」と頼む場面を考えます。AIエージェントは検索、比較、表の作成までを一続きで進めます。 ゴールを渡せば手順まで任せられる という性質を押さえると、この後に紹介する種類の違いも理解しやすくなります。 生成AIとAIエージェントの違い 生成AIは指示に応じて文章や画像を作るAIです。一方でAIエージェントは、生成AIを頭脳として使い、 作業そのものを最後まで進める仕組み です。 比較項目 生成AI AIエージェント 主な役割 文章・画像・コードなどを生成する 目標の達成に向けて作業を進める 指示の出し方 1回の指示に1回の出力を返す ゴールを伝えると手順を自分で組み立てる 外部ツールの利用 基本的に会話の中で完結する 検索・API・ファイル操作などを使う 人の役割 出力を受け取り、次の指示を考える 途中経過や最終結果を確認する 生成AIの出力を人が次の作業につなげていた部分を、AIエージェントは自分で引き受けます。そのため、複数の手順にまたがる業務ほど効果が出やすくなります。 ChatGPTやGeminiのように、生成AIのサービスにエージェント機能が組み込まれる例も多くあります。同じサービス名でも、使う機能によって生成AIにもAIエージェントにもなります。 「作る」のが生成AI、「進める」のがAIエージェントと区別しておくと、社内で違いを説明するときにも迷いません。 動作の仕組みによるAIエージェントの種類5つ IBMは、AIエージェントを動作の仕組みによって以下の5つに分類しています。 出典： AIエージェントの種類（IBM） 単純反射型エージェント モデルベース反射型エージェント 目標ベース型エージェント 効用ベース型エージェント 学習エージェント 学術的な分類ですが、サービスがどこまで自分で判断できるのかを見極める物差しになります。 単純反射型エージェント 単純反射型エージェントは、 今の入力だけを見て、決められたルールどおりに動く もっともシンプルな種類です。過去の出来事や行動の結果は考慮しません。 記憶も環境のモデルも持たないため、処理が速く、動作を予測しやすい点が長所です。ただし、ルールにない状況や、入力だけでは状況がわからない環境には対応できません。 IBMは、設定温度を下回ると暖房をつけるサーモスタットを例に挙げています。業務でいえば、特定のキーワードに定型文を返すだけのチャットボットがこの種類に近いでしょう。 自社の業務が「条件と対応が1対1で決まっている」なら、高度なAIエージェントでなくても、この種類の仕組みで十分なケースがあります。 モデルベース反射型エージェント モデルベース反射型エージェントは、ルールで動く点は単純反射型と同じです。違いは、 過去の情報から作った環境の内部モデルを持っている 点です。 内部モデルがあるため、今の入力だけでは見えない状況も、それまでの記録から推測できます。ルールの外に出る判断はできませんが、単純反射型より多くの場面に対応します。 IBMは、すでに通った場所や障害物を覚えながら部屋を移動するロボットを例に挙げています。業務では、会話の履歴を踏まえて回答を変える問い合わせ対応が近い動きをします。 過去のやり取りを踏まえる必要がある業務では、記憶を持つかどうかが種類を見分ける最初の判断材料になります。 目標ベース型エージェント 目標ベース型エージェントは、 設定された目標から逆算して行動を選ぶ 種類です。行動の前に、どの選択肢が目標に近づくかを評価します。 ルールに従うだけの反射型と違い、目標が同じなら状況に応じて手順を変えられます。計画を立て、途中で結果を見ながら次の一手を決める点が特徴です。 IBMは、建物内の特定の部屋まで遠回りせずに進む経路を計画するロボットを例に挙げています。「バグを直す」というゴールから調査と修正を進めるコーディング用のAIエージェントも、この考え方に近い動き方です。 現在よく使われるAIエージェントの多くは、この目標ベース型を土台に考えると理解しやすくなります。 効用ベース型エージェント 効用ベース型エージェントは、目標を達成できるかだけでなく、 結果の「望ましさ」を数値で比べて最善の行動を選ぶ 種類です。この望ましさを測る基準を効用関数と呼びます。 目標を達成する方法が複数あり、速さ・コスト・安全性などを両立させる必要がある場面で力を発揮します。目標ベース型が「達成できるか」を見るのに対し、効用ベース型は「どれだけよいか」まで見ます。 IBMは、移動時間・燃費・安全性を比べながら走る自動運転車や、販売履歴と在庫から価格を決めるECの例を挙げています。 価格設定や配送計画など、複数の条件の折り合いをつける業務を任せたい場合に、この種類の考え方が当てはまります。 学習エージェント 学習エージェントは、 環境からのフィードバックをもとに、自分の行動を改善し続ける 種類です。最初から完璧である必要はなく、使うほど精度が上がります。 IBMによると、学習エージェントは以下の4つの要素で構成されます。 行動を実行する性能要素 改善を担う学習要素 結果を評価する批評要素 新しい行動を試させる問題生成要素 例としては、報酬と罰を手がかりに学ぶ強化学習のエージェントや、SNSのおすすめ表示などが挙げられています。 環境の変化が大きい業務では、導入後に改善していける仕組みがあるかを確認すると、長く使えるAIエージェントを選べます。 システム構成によるAIエージェントの種類2つ AIエージェントは、何体で動かすかによってシングルエージェントとマルチエージェントの2つに分かれます。任せたい業務の複雑さによって、向いている構成が変わります。 シングルエージェント シングルエージェントは、 1体のAIエージェントが業務の最初から最後までを担当する 構成です。 構成がシンプルなため、作りやすく、問題が起きたときに原因を追いやすい点が長所です。ただし、扱う情報や工程が増えるほど、1体ですべてを正確に処理するのは難しくなります。 たとえば、社内規程についての質問に答える、受け取ったメールを要約するといった業務はシングルエージェントで十分に対応できます。 初めてAIエージェントを試すなら、まずシングルエージェントで小さな業務を任せると、効果と課題を早く確かめられます。 マルチエージェント マルチエージェントは、 役割の違う複数のAIエージェントが分担して1つの業務を進める 構成です。富士通は、役割を以下の3つに分けて説明しています。 出典： AIエージェント（富士通） ワーカーAIエージェント：個別のタスクを実行する オーケストレーターAIエージェント：ワーカーを選んで連携させる司令塔 ヴェリファイヤーAIエージェント：出力を検証して信頼性を高める 上位のエージェントが全体の目標を受け持ち、下位のエージェントが具体的な作業を担う形は、階層型エージェントとも呼ばれます。IBMも、複雑な問題を小さなタスクに分ける仕組みとして紹介しています。 調査・執筆・事実確認のように工程が分かれた業務では、マルチエージェントにすると各工程の品質を保ちやすくなります。 用途によるAIエージェントの種類6つ 任せる業務で分けると、AIエージェントは以下の6種類に整理できます。 業務自動化型 情報検索・ナレッジ型 カスタマー対応型 コーディング支援型 リサーチ型 ブラウザ操作型 自社で困っている業務がどれに当てはまるかを考えると、候補のサービスが見つけやすくなります。※サービス情報は2026年10月時点のものです。 業務自動化型 業務自動化型は、 資料作成・データ入力・報告書の作成など、手順の決まった定型業務を自動で進める 種類です。 人が毎回同じ手順でこなしている作業ほど効果が出やすく、担当者は確認や判断に時間を回せます。複数のアプリやファイルをまたぐ作業もまとめて任せられます。 代表例は、JAPAN AI株式会社の「JAPAN AI AGENT」です。業務ごとに用意されたエージェントを使えるほか、自社用のエージェントも作成できます。 OpenAIの「ChatGPT Work」も、つながっているアプリやファイルを使って、文書・表・スライドなどを作るエージェントです。以前の「ChatGPT agent」は提供を終え、ChatGPT Workに引き継がれています。 > JAPAN AI AGENTの発表はこちらから > ChatGPT Workの公式サイトはこちらから 情報検索・ナレッジ型 情報検索・ナレッジ型は、 社内の文書やデータから必要な情報を探し、根拠つきで回答する 種類です。 社内規程・マニュアル・過去の提案書などが複数のツールに散らばっている企業ほど、探す時間を減らせます。回答の根拠となる文書を示してくれるため、内容の確認もしやすくなります。 代表例は「Glean」です。社内のさまざまなツールを横断して検索でき、業務を進めるエージェントも作成できます。 Microsoftの「Researcher」は、社内のデータとWebの情報を組み合わせ、複数の手順が必要な調査をこなすエージェントです。 > Gleanの公式ドキュメントはこちらから > Researcherの公式ドキュメントはこちらから カスタマー対応型 カスタマー対応型は、 顧客からの問い合わせに答え、必要な手続きまで進める 種類です。 従来のチャットボットは決められた回答を返すだけでした。カスタマー対応型のAIエージェントは、顧客情報を確認し、返品の受付などの処理まで担います。 代表例は、Salesforceの「Agentforce」です。CRMの顧客データを使い、営業やサポートの業務をこなします。 Zendeskの「AIエージェント」は、問い合わせの解決に特化したエージェントです。対応の手順を自然言語で設定できます。 > Agentforceの公式サイトはこちらから > ZendeskのAIエージェントの公式サイトはこちらから コーディング支援型 コーディング支援型は、 コードの読み取り・編集・テストの実行まで進める 開発者向けの種類です。 コードの続きを提案する補完ツールと違い、機能の追加やバグの修正といったタスク単位で作業を任せられます。 主なサービスは以下の3つです。 Claude agent」という名称でした。開発チームの人手不足に悩む企業では、定型的な実装を任せてレビューに時間を回せます。 > Claude Codeの公式ドキュメントはこちらから > Copilot cloud agentの公式ドキュメントはこちらから > Devinの公式サイトはこちらから リサーチ型 リサーチ型は、 Web上の多数の情報源を調べ、出典つきのレポートにまとめる 種類です。 items.title: Push-based KV transfer to improve TTFT and TPOT for disaggregated inference in vLLM
items.description: vLLM is an open-source inference and serving engine for large language models (LLMs). LLM inference has two distinct phases: prefill, which processes the input prompt and builds the key-value (KV) cache, and decode, which uses that cache to generate output one token at a time. These phases have different compute, memory, and scaling characteristics. Prefill-decode (P-D) disaggregation runs them on separate engine instances, allowing each phase to scale and be optimized independently. This can improve resource utilization, throughput, and latency under load. However, it also requires transferring the KV cache from the prefill instance to the decode instance before token generation can begin, making efficient KV transfer critical to time-to-first-token (TTFT). One of the ways vLLM performs this transfer is through the NVIDIA Inference Xfer Library (NIXL) connector , which moves KV blocks over interconnects that support Remote Direct Memory Access (RDMA), such as AWS Elastic Fabric Adapter ( AWS EFA , the low-latency RDMA network used across servers in AWS). On supported instance types , AWS EFA supports GPUDirect RDMA and Neuron Direct RDMA. NIXL can therefore transfer KV blocks directly between GPU or AWS Trainium device memory without staging through host memory. The default mode for NIXL connector is pull-based : After the prefill instance finishes computing the prompt KV cache, the router relays the source metadata, including the prefill block IDs, to the decode instance. The decode instance then allocates destination blocks, prepares the NIXL transfer, and initiates NIXL READ to pull the KV blocks from the prefill instance. Because these coordination and setup steps occur sequentially after prefill and before decoding can begin, they extend the TTFT critical path, as shown in the following timeline. Figure 1: Pull-mode KV transfer timeline, where the router relay, decode-side allocation, and NIXL READ run serially on the path to the first token This post introduces a push-based NIXL connector that moves post-prefill transfer coordination and setup off the critical path. If you run disaggregated prefill/decode inference with vLLM, push mode can improve application responsiveness by reducing TTFT and TPOT, particularly at high request rates. In our benchmark on a 1P1D deployment using Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) P5en instances connected with EFA, push mode delivered up to 3x better TTFT and up to 30 percent better time-per-output-token (TPOT) compared to pull mode (see the Performance data section) for the Qwen3-32B model. Results depend on workload and configuration. We built and validated the feature on AWS Trainium instance clusters connected with EFA, and then we contributed it to vLLM as an accelerator-agnostic feature. The results here are from an Amazon EC2 P5en (GPU) cluster with EFA, showing the gains carry over to GPUs. This post explains the push-based architecture, transfer flow, threading model, performance results, and how to reproduce the benchmark. Push-based KV transfer This section explains the push-based design: its architecture, the transfer protocol, and the threading model that keeps KV transfer off the critical path. Architecture overview Push-based transfer improves TTFT and decode throughput for two reasons: It removes the serialization of the pull model by overlapping producer and consumer work. The decode instance registers its target blocks in advance while the producer is still computing KV. The transfer then begins as soon as the producer’s blocks are ready, rather than after a consumer-side ID-discovery round trip, removing that round trip from the path to first token. It moves the transfer-setup time off the decode instance. That setup runs on the prefill side and on a background thread. It prepares the NIXL descriptors and submits the transfer, so the decode instance does not spend those cycles during its latency-critical token-generation phase. The net effect is lower TTFT and higher output-token throughput on the decode instance. The push connector coordinates three actors: the decode instance registers its target blocks up front, the prefill instance matches each request and issues the transfer, and a dedicated background thread carries the KV write off the engine’s forward-pass loop. The following diagram shows how these pieces fit together. Figure 2: Push-based KV transfer architecture, showing how the decode instance, prefill instance, and background transfer thread coordinate Implementation details The protocol has three logical steps. 1. Registration (decode side). When the decode instance allocates local blocks for a request requiring remote prefilling, it prepares a registration describing where the prefill instance should write the KV: its own identity and the block locations it has just reserved. Within the same engine step, the worker transmits this registration to the prefill instance as a NIXL notification. Because registration happens at allocation time, the connector knows the destination blocks before the prefill instance completes prefill. 2. Rendezvous (prefill side). The registration from the decoder and the completion of prefill on the producer can arrive in either order, and the connector handles both. If the registration arrives first, the producer holds it until its own prefill finishes. If prefill finishes first, the producer holds the request’s blocks until the registration arrives. Whichever event happens second triggers the transfer. The connector pairs requests by ID, and the matching accounts for reissued requests, correctly associating preempted or retried requests. 3. Transfer (prefill side). Once a request is matched, the producer establishes a connection to the decode instance (if one does not already exist) and issues an NIXL WRITE that copies the KV blocks directly into the decoder’s registered memory, addressing each destination tensor-parallel rank. items.title: Improve TTFT for multi-turn agentic workloads with bi-directional KV transfer in vLLM
items.description: Multi-turn agentic workloads build on accumulated context as an agent reasons, invokes tools, and incorporates earlier results. With each new turn, the client resends the conversation history, including system instructions, prior prompts, tool results, and model responses, causing the growing context to be processed repeatedly. In Prefill-decode (P-D) disaggregation , each request is split across specialized nodes: the prefill node processes the prompt and builds its key-value (KV) cache, then the decode node retrieves those KV blocks and generates the response. Conventional disaggregated serving, however, only transfers KV cache in one direction: from prefill to decode node. This one-directional flow creates two inefficiencies for multi-turn workloads. First, after generating a response, the decode node holds KV cache entries for both the prompt and the newly generated tokens. When processing the next turn, the prefill node cannot retrieve those entries, so it must recompute the KV projections for the previous response tokens. Second, the decode node maintains the session state while the prefill nodes don’t, increasing the probability of cache eviction for active sessions on the prefill nodes. On a full cache miss, the prefill node must recompute KV projections for the entire conversation history, including system instructions, prior user requests, tool results, and model-generated responses. As the conversation grows, this redundant work consumes more accelerator capacity and increases time to first token (TTFT). When you build conversational assistants and agentic applications, longer interaction histories can increase latency and consume accelerator capacity through repeated prefill computation. In this post, we show how bi-directional KV cache transfer lets prefill and decode nodes reuse previously computed context across turns, which improves accelerator utilization and helps applications sustain responsive TTFT as conversations grow. In our multi-turn benchmarks on a 1P1D deployment using Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) P5en instances, bi-directional KV transfer reduced TTFT by up to 1.6x for Qwen3-32B and up to 3.3x for zai-org/GLM-5-FP8 (see the Performance data section). Results vary with workload and configuration. The instances are connected with AWS Elastic Fabric Adapter ( AWS EFA ), a low-latency remote direct memory access (RDMA) network used across servers in AWS. On supported instance types , AWS EFA supports GPUDirect RDMA and Neuron Direct RDMA to move KV blocks directly between GPU or AWS Trainium device memory on the prefill and decode nodes. We originally built and validated the feature on AWS Trainium instance clusters connected with EFA and contributed it to vLLM as an accelerator-agnostic capability. The results presented here are from an Amazon EC2 P5en GPU cluster with EFA, showing that the benefits also carry over to GPUs. This post explains the bi-directional KV transfer architecture, router metadata flow, KV-block retention and recompute controls, performance results, and how to reproduce the benchmark. Bi-directional KV transfer Bi-directional KV transfer is a mechanism in which a decode node returns previously computed KV to a prefill node on subsequent turns of a conversation. This avoids recomputing shared context on the prefill node and is governed by a configurable KV recompute threshold. It mitigates both computational-redundancy scenarios described earlier. To make it work, the KV must survive past the turn that produced it and travel in the reverse direction, coordinated by a KV-cache-aware router. NIXL KV connector enhancements for bi-directional transfer We extended the NVIDIA Inference Xfer Library (NIXL) KV connector to let prefill nodes consume remote KV blocks, similar to how decode nodes already consume KV blocks that the prefill node provides. This is not a trivial change, because the two node types are architecturally different: prefill nodes compute KV representations for new prompt tokens and can provide complete prompt KV blocks. Decode nodes lack the capability (or efficiency) to generate complete KV representations and can only serve previously cached KV blocks. As a result, prefill and decode nodes still carry their own roles and logic for computing the metadata of remote and local KV blocks. The actual KV transfer mechanism (a NIXL READ), however, is common to both the P->D and D->P directions. The following diagram first shows the existing flow in blue. The router sends the request to prefill node, prefill node computes the prompt KV and returns its block metadata, and the router forwards the request and metadata to decode node for the standard P→D NIXL READ. The numbered red path illustrates the bi-directional KV transfer additions: (1) decode node retains eligible KV blocks after generation, (2) returns their metadata in the streaming response, and (3) the router caches that metadata for the next prefill request. Prefill node then (4) checks the remotely reusable KV after it applies local cache matches, (5) queues an asynchronous receive when the reusable token count meets the threshold, and (6) performs a D→P NIXL READ before computing the remaining suffix. Figure 1: Standard prefill-to-decode flow (blue) and the bi-directional KV transfer additions (red) KV-cache-aware router vLLM includes connector-side support for bi-directional KV transfer, while coordinating KV reuse across conversation turns requires a KV-cache-aware router. vLLM GitHub provides an example proxy that implements the flow used in this post which can be adapted for your environment. The KV-cache-aware router is a lightweight, stateful control-plane component between the client, prefill, and decode nodes. It maintains an in-memory mapping from the client-provided conversation_id to decode’s kv_transfer_params . items.title: The Thin Orchestrator: How We Made Our AI Agents More Reliable by Giving the Router Less to Do
items.description: Sometimes, giving an AI agent all of the knowledge it needs is the wrong approach. At Meta, we’ve seen notable improvements in efficiency and accuracy by keeping the orchestration layer of our data pipeline agents deliberately thin: It routes work and enforces reliability checks, while specialized agents do the domain reasoning. We’re sharing our own process and insights, plus how any team can apply this to their production AI agents. We built a 1,300-line orchestrator that routes 20+ workflows to 14 specialized AI agents. It performs zero domain work itself. That’s the point. When we first deployed AI agents to automate data column onboarding across Meta’s recommendation systems — a process spanning three code repositories, three programming languages, and up to six pipeline stages that must stay in sync — we did what most teams do: We built one smart agent that knew everything. It worked in demos. In production, it started hallucinating. The fix wasn’t better prompts or a bigger context window. It was giving the central agent less to do. We call this the thin orchestrator pattern: a router that owns sequencing and reliability checks, and leaves every domain decision to specialists. The Problem: More Context, Worse Results Our pipeline is config-as-code: Python configurations drive C++ code generation, which feeds data processing services, which populate analytics systems. Onboarding a single data column requires coordinated changes across configuration registries, backend services, and data pipelines, and each column moves through up to six stages before its data arrives. Our first approach was a single AI agent loaded with all domain knowledge, configuration schemas, code generation rules, pipeline routing logic, validation requirements, and population patterns for 10+ data sources. The agent had everything it needed. That was the problem. Past a certain context threshold, additional knowledge degraded rather than improved performance. The agent would cross-contaminate concepts, applying field naming conventions from one subsystem to another, or using a code generation pattern meant for one data source when populating from a different one. A preprint from the Windreich Department of Artificial Intelligence and Human Health at Mount Sinai found that orchestrated multiagent systems held 65.3% accuracy at 80-task batches where single agents fell to 16.6%, while reducing token usage up to 65-fold. The authors attribute this to the design’s isolation of tasks, which prevented context interference. We were experiencing the inverse, a single agent drowning in its own knowledge. We also evaluated an alternative single-agent approach. Its success rate was 70-80% with manual prompt engineering per task: An engineer had to craft a custom system prompt for each specific job. Without that handholding, success dropped to 10-20%. This wasn’t a prompt engineering problem. It was an architectural one. The Approach: A Thin Router With Specialist Workers We split the system into two layers: A deterministic orchestrator that performs zero domain work. It classifies intent, gathers required fields, runs reliability checks, and delegates to the right specialist. It never reasons about code, never generates configurations, and never touches the codebase. It’s a router. Fourteen specialized subagents , each a complete domain expert with isolated context. A schema management agent knows configuration registries. A population agent knows how to generate code for each of 10 data sources. A validation agent knows build systems and quality checks. No agent sees the full picture. That’s the feature, not the bug. The orchestrator follows a fixed 7-step protocol for every request: Read the relevant subagent’s instruction file. Check if the target already exists (prevent duplicates). Gather required fields from the user. Auto-discover what can be inferred (repository type, existing configurations). Reliability gate check for active warnings or required reviewers. Delegate to the subagent with full context. Handle results and surface errors, confirm success. Steps 1–5 and 7 are deterministic. Only step 6 involves large language model (LLM) reasoning, and it happens inside an isolated subagent with only its domain knowledge loaded. What We Built: Workflow Templates, Not New Agents One architectural insight was separating what needs to happen from how each step is performed. The orchestrator defines phase ordering through workflow templates — deterministic state machines that constrain the LLM’s decision space: Column Onboarding: Schema → Validation → Population → Testing Event Onboarding: Schema → Population → Validation → Testing → Event Processing Pipeline Migration: Assessment → Planning → Population → Validation → Monitoring Each workflow template reuses the same pool of 14 subagents in different sequences. When we needed to support pipeline migration, a completely new use case, we didn’t build new agents. We wrote a new workflow template that sequenced existing agents differently. Zero new agent code. Full production capability. Each subagent follows a standardized structure: Knowledge sources: which domain files to load at runtime (typically a few thousand tokens each). Pre-gathering checklist: what the orchestrator must collect before delegation. Step-by-step workflow: the domain-specific execution plan. Discovery patterns: how to find relevant code patterns in the monorepo. Troubleshooting: error-to-resolution mappings for common failures. This uniformity means adding a new subagent is templated work, not greenfield engineering. The 15th subagent looks structurally identical to the first. Knowledge files are loaded on demand at subagent execution time, not embedded in the orchestrator. We maintain 25+ knowledge files organized by workflow domain.
